parts.problemMd:
Find the probability that, in the sample of 30 light bulbs,

(i) exactly one light bulb has a lifetime of less than 5000 hours,

(ii) no more than three light bulbs have a lifetime of less than 5000 hours.
parts.solutionMd:
(i)

Let $X$ be the number of bulbs in the sample with a lifetime of less than 5000 hours

`X \sim \text{B}(30, \; 0.1)`

Use `\text{P}(X = r) = {}^{n}C_{r} \, p^{r}\left(1 - p\right)^{n - r}` with $r = 1$

`\text{P}(X = 1) = {}^{30}C_{1}(0.1)\left(0.9\right)^{29}`

**[M1]**

$\text{P} ( X = 1 ) = 0 . 141303 \dots$

**Final answer:** $\text{P} ( X = 1 ) = 0 . 141$** (3 s.f.)**

**[A1]**

(ii)

"No more than three" means $X = 0$, 1, 2 or 3, so add those four terms

`\text{P}(X \leq 3) = \left(0.9\right)^{30} + {}^{30}C_{1}(0.1)\left(0.9\right)^{29} + {}^{30}C_{2}\left(0.1\right)^{2}\left(0.9\right)^{28} + {}^{30}C_{3}\left(0.1\right)^{3}\left(0.9\right)^{27}`

**[M1 A1]**

$\text{P} ( X \leq 3 ) = 0 . 647439 \dots$

**Final answer:** $\text{P} ( X \leq 3 ) = 0 . 647$** (3 s.f.)**

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: `{}^{30}C_{1}(0.1)\left(0.9\right)^{29}`, or 30 × 0.1 × 0.9²⁹.
> 
> **A1**: 0.141, or answers which round to 0.141.
> 
> **M1**: At least one binomial term of the form `{}^{30}C_{x}\left(0.1\right)^{x}\left(0.9\right)^{30 - x}`.
> 
> **A1**: A correct expression for P(X ≤ 3), written in full with no terms missing. Accept unsimplified.
> 
> **B1**: 0.647, or answers which round to 0.647.
> 
> If 0.141 or 0.647 is given with no working, for example straight from a calculator, award 1 mark only for that answer.

parts.problemMd:
Abner, an American baseball fan, has just moved to a town in which it is known that 85% of the residents are familiar with the rules of the game.

Abner takes a random sample of 40 residents of the town. Find the probability that

(i) fewer than 38

(ii) no more than 38

(iii) more than 38

(iv) at most 38 but at least 36

of the residents in Abner's sample are familiar with the rules of baseball.
parts.solutionMd:
(i)

The 40 residents are a random sample, so they are independent, each with the same probability 0.85 of being familiar with the rules, and $X$, the number who are, follows a binomial distribution

`X \sim \text{B}(40, \; 0.85)`

Fewer than 38 means $X \leq 37$. The upper tail $X = 38$, 39, 40 is much shorter, so subtract it from 1

`\text{P}(X < 38) = 1 - \left[\text{P}(X = 38) + \text{P}(X = 39) + \text{P}(X = 40)\right]`

`\text{P}(X < 38) = 1 - \left[{}^{40}C_{38}\left(0.85\right)^{38}\left(0.15\right)^{2} + {}^{40}C_{39}\left(0.85\right)^{39}(0.15) + \left(0.85\right)^{40}\right]`

**[M1]**

$\text{P} ( X < 38 ) = 1 - ( 0 . 0364918 \dots + 0 . 0106044 \dots + 0 . 0015023 \dots ) = 1 - 0 . 0485986 \dots$

**Final answer:** $\text{P} ( X < 38 ) = 0 . 951$** (3 s.f.)**

**[A1]**

(ii)

No more than 38 means $X \leq 38$, so only $X = 39$ and $X = 40$ are excluded

$\text{P} ( X \leq 38 ) = 1 - ( 0 . 0106044 \dots + 0 . 0015023 \dots ) = 1 - 0 . 0121067 \dots = 0 . 987893 \dots$

**Final answer:** $\text{P} ( X \leq 38 ) = 0 . 988$** (3 s.f.)**

**[B1]**

(iii)

More than 38 means $X = 39$ or $X = 40$, the two terms just excluded in (ii)

$\text{P} ( X > 38 ) = 0 . 0106044 \dots + 0 . 0015023 \dots = 0 . 0121067 \dots$

**Final answer:** $\text{P} ( X > 38 ) = 0 . 0121$** (3 s.f.)**

**[B1]**

(iv)

At least 36 but at most 38 means $X = 36$, 37 or 38

`\text{P}(36 \leq X \leq 38) = {}^{40}C_{36}\left(0.85\right)^{36}\left(0.15\right)^{4} + {}^{40}C_{37}\left(0.85\right)^{37}\left(0.15\right)^{3} + {}^{40}C_{38}\left(0.85\right)^{38}\left(0.15\right)^{2}`

$\text{P} ( 36 \leq X \leq 38 ) = 0 . 251213 \dots$

**Final answer:** $\text{P} ( 36 \leq X \leq 38 ) = 0 . 251$** (3 s.f.)**

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: A correct expression for P(X < 38): 1 minus the terms for 38, 39 and 40, or the sum of the terms from 0 to 37. Accept unsimplified.
> 
> **A1**: 0.951, or answers which round to 0.951.
> 
> **B1**: P(X ≤ 38) = 0.988, or answers which round to 0.988.
> 
> **B1**: P(X > 38) = 0.0121, or answers which round to 0.0121.
> 
> **B1**: P(36 ≤ X ≤ 38) = 0.251, or answers which round to 0.251.
> 
> If 0.951 is given with no working, for example straight from a calculator, award 1 mark only.

parts.problemMd:
Farmer Kate has a herd of 50 alpacas. From previous testing of the herd, she knows that each alpaca has a probability of 0.95 of testing negative for tuberculosis (TB). She chooses a random sample of 8 alpacas from the herd and tests them for TB.

$N$ is the number of alpacas in the sample that test negative for TB, and $T$ is the number of alpacas in the sample that test positive for TB.

(i) State the distribution of $N$, giving the values of its parameters.

(ii) State the distribution of $T$, giving the values of its parameters.
parts.solutionMd:
(i)

The 8 alpacas are independent, each with the same probability 0.95 of testing negative, so $N$ follows a binomial distribution

`N \sim \text{B}(8, \; 0.95)`

**[B1]**

(ii)

Each alpaca that does not test negative tests positive, with probability $1 - 0 . 95 = 0 . 05$

`T \sim \text{B}(8, \; 0.05)`

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: B(8, 0.95), or "binomial with n = 8 and p = 0.95".
> 
> **B1**: B(8, 0.05), or "binomial with n = 8 and p = 0.05".
> 
> Both parameters are needed for each mark. The two distributions are marked independently.

parts.problemMd:
Find the probability that the number of alpacas in the sample that test positive for TB is

(i) zero,

(ii) more than 2.
parts.solutionMd:
(i)

Use `T \sim \text{B}(8, \; 0.05)`: none positive means all 8 test negative

`\text{P}(T = 0) = \left(0.95\right)^{8} = 0.663420\ldots`

**Final answer:** $\text{P} ( T = 0 ) = 0 . 663$** (3 s.f.)**

**[B1]**

(ii)

$T > 2$ is every outcome except $T = 0$, 1 or 2, so subtract those three terms from 1

`\text{P}(T > 2) = 1 - \left[\left(0.95\right)^{8} + {}^{8}C_{1}(0.05)\left(0.95\right)^{7} + {}^{8}C_{2}\left(0.05\right)^{2}\left(0.95\right)^{6}\right]`

**[M1 A1]**

$\text{P} ( T > 2 ) = 1 - 0 . 994211 \dots = 0 . 005788 \dots$

**Final answer:** $\text{P} ( T > 2 ) = 0 . 00579$** (3 s.f.)**

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: 0.663, or answers which round to 0.663.
> 
> **M1**: At least one binomial term of the form `{}^{8}C_{x}\left(0.05\right)^{x}\left(0.95\right)^{8 - x}`.
> 
> **A1**: A correct expression for P(T > 2), written in full with no terms missing: 1 minus the terms for 0, 1 and 2, or the sum of the six terms from 3 to 8. Accept unsimplified.
> 
> **B1**: 0.00579, or answers which round to 0.00579.
> 
> Working with N instead of T is equally valid (more than 2 positive is fewer than 6 negative).
> 
> If 0.00579 is given with no working, for example straight from a calculator, award 1 mark only.

parts.problemMd: Find the probability that the die lands on a 4 exactly four times.
parts.solutionMd:
The die is fair, so the probability of a 4 on each roll is $\frac{1}{6}$

`X \sim \text{B}\left(24, \; \dfrac{1}{6}\right)`

parts.problemMd:

`\text{P}(X = 45) = {}^{50}C_{45}\left(0.92\right)^{45}\left(0.08\right)^{5}`

parts.problemMd:
The probability that a seed of a certain variety fails to germinate is 0.15, independently of other seeds. A random sample of 40 of these seeds is planted. The random variable $X$ is the number of these seeds that fail to germinate.

Find

(i) $\text{E} ( X )$,

(ii) $\text{Var} ( X )$.
parts.solutionMd:
(i)

The 40 seeds are independent, each with the same probability 0.15 of failing to germinate, so $X$ follows a binomial distribution

`X \sim \text{B}(40, \; 0.15)`

Use $\text{E} ( X ) = n p$

$\text{E} ( X ) = 40 \times 0 . 15$

$\text{E} ( X ) = 6$

**[B1]**

(ii)

Use $\text{Var} ( X ) = n p ( 1 - p )$

$\text{Var} ( X ) = 40 \times 0 . 15 \times 0 . 85$

$\text{Var} ( X ) = 5 . 1$

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: E(X) = 6.
> 
> **B1**: Var(X) = 5.1.

parts.problemMd:
Find the probability that

(i) exactly 5 of the seeds fail to germinate,

(ii) at least 3 of the seeds fail to germinate.
parts.solutionMd:
(i)

Use `\text{P}(X = r) = {}^{n}C_{r} \, p^{r}\left(1 - p\right)^{n - r}` with $r = 5$

`\text{P}(X = 5) = {}^{40}C_{5}\left(0.15\right)^{5}\left(0.85\right)^{35}`

**[M1]**

$\text{P} ( X = 5 ) = 0 . 169180 \dots$

**Final answer:** $\text{P} ( X = 5 ) = 0 . 169$** (3 s.f.)**

**[A1]**

(ii)

At least 3 is every outcome except $X = 0$, 1 or 2, so subtract those three terms from 1

`\text{P}(X \geq 3) = 1 - \left[\left(0.85\right)^{40} + {}^{40}C_{1}(0.15)\left(0.85\right)^{39} + {}^{40}C_{2}\left(0.15\right)^{2}\left(0.85\right)^{38}\right]`

**[M1]**

$\text{P} ( X \geq 3 ) = 1 - 0 . 0485986 \dots = 0 . 951401 \dots$

**Final answer:** $\text{P} ( X \geq 3 ) = 0 . 951$** (3 s.f.)**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: `{}^{40}C_{5}\left(0.15\right)^{5}\left(0.85\right)^{35}`.
> 
> **A1**: 0.169, or answers which round to 0.169.
> 
> **M1**: 1 − [P(0) + P(1) + P(2)], with all three terms correct. Accept unsimplified.
> 
> **A1**: 0.951, or answers which round to 0.951.
> 
> If 0.169 or 0.951 is given with no working, for example straight from a calculator, award 1 mark only for that answer.

parts.problemMd: Given that at least 3 of the seeds fail to germinate, find the probability that exactly 5 of them fail to germinate.
parts.solutionMd:
Use the definition of conditional probability

`\text{P}(X = 5 \mid X \geq 3) = \dfrac{\text{P}(X = 5 \cap X \geq 3)}{\text{P}(X \geq 3)}`

$X = 5$ already satisfies $X \geq 3$, so the numerator is just $\text{P} ( X = 5 )$. Use the unrounded answers to (b)

`\text{P}(X = 5 \mid X \geq 3) = \dfrac{0.169180\ldots}{0.951401\ldots}`

**[M1]**

`\text{P}(X = 5 \mid X \geq 3) = 0.177822\ldots`

**Final answer:** `\text{P}(X = 5 \mid X \geq 3) = 0.178`** (3 s.f.)**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: P(X = 5) divided by P(X ≥ 3), using the answers to (b) or correct values. Both numerator and denominator must be seen.
> 
> **A1**: 0.178, or answers which round to 0.178.

parts.problemMd:
The random variable `X \sim \text{Geo}(p)`.

(i) Find the value of $p$ when $\text{P} ( X \geq 3 ) = 0 . 09$.

(ii) Find the possible values of $p$ when $\text{P} ( X = 2 ) = 0 . 2275$.
parts.solutionMd:
(i)

$X \geq 3$ means the first 2 trials are both failures

`\text{P}(X \geq 3) = \text{P}(X > 2) = \left(1 - p\right)^{2}`

`\left(1 - p\right)^{2} = 0.09`

**[M1]**

Take the square root of both sides

$1 - p = 0 . 3$* or *$1 - p = - 0 . 3$

$1 - p$ is a probability, so it cannot be negative

$p = 0 . 7$

**[A1]**

(ii)

Use `\text{P}(X = r) = p\left(1 - p\right)^{r - 1}` with $r = 2$

$p ( 1 - p ) = 0 . 2275$

**[M1]**

Rearrange into a quadratic in $p$

$p^{2} - p + 0 . 2275 = 0$

Solve, using the quadratic formula

$p = \frac{1\pm\sqrt{1-4(0.2275)}}{2} = \frac{1\pm0.3}{2}$

**Final answer:** $p = 0 . 35$** or **$p = 0 . 65$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: `\left(1 - p\right)^{2} = 0.09`.
> 
> **A1**: p = 0.7 only. The value 1.3 must be rejected, or not given.
> 
> **M1**: $p ( 1 - p ) = 0 . 2275$.
> 
> **A1**: p = 0.35 and p = 0.65. Both values are needed. Accept solving by factorising or completing the square.

parts.problemMd:
The random variable `Y \sim \text{B}(5, \; p)`.

(i) Find the value of $p$ when $\text{E} ( Y ) = 3$.

(ii) Find the value of $p$ when $\text{P} ( Y = 5 ) = 0 . 32768$.

(iii) Find the possible values of $p$ when $\text{Var} ( Y ) = 1 . 05$.
parts.solutionMd:
(i)

Use $\text{E} ( Y ) = n p$ with $n = 5$

$5 p = 3$

$p = 0 . 6$

**[B1]**

(ii)

$Y = 5$ means all 5 trials are successes

`\text{P}(Y = 5) = {}^{5}C_{5} \, p^{5}\left(1 - p\right)^{0} = p^{5}`

$p^{5} = 0 . 32768$

`p = \left(0.32768\right)^{\frac{1}{5}}`

$p = 0 . 8$

**[B1]**

(iii)

Use $\text{Var} ( Y ) = n p ( 1 - p )$ with $n = 5$

$5 p ( 1 - p ) = 1 . 05$

**[M1]**

Divide by 5 and rearrange into a quadratic in $p$

$p^{2} - p + 0 . 21 = 0$

Factorise

$( p - 0 . 3 ) ( p - 0 . 7 ) = 0$

**[M1]**

**Final answer:** $p = 0 . 3$** or **$p = 0 . 7$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: p = 0.6.
> 
> **B1**: p = 0.8.
> 
> **M1**: $5 p ( 1 - p ) = 1 . 05$.
> 
> **M1**: Solving the resulting three-term quadratic by any valid method.
> 
> **A1**: p = 0.3 and p = 0.7. Both values are needed.

parts.problemMd:
Guglielma rolls a biased die for which the probability of landing on a 5 on any roll is $\frac{2}{11}$, independently of other rolls.

Find the probability that Guglielma rolls a 5 for the first time on her 21st roll.
parts.solutionMd:
The rolls are independent, each with the same probability $\frac{2}{11}$ of a 5, so $X$, the number of rolls up to and including the first 5, follows a geometric distribution

`X \sim \text{Geo}\left(\dfrac{2}{11}\right)`

Use `\text{P}(X = r) = p\left(1 - p\right)^{r - 1}`: the first 20 rolls are not a 5, then the 21st is

`\text{P}(X = 21) = \left(\dfrac{9}{11}\right)^{20}\left(\dfrac{2}{11}\right)`

**[M1]**

$\text{P} ( X = 21 ) = 0 . 00328574 \dots$

**Final answer:** $\text{P} ( X = 21 ) = 0 . 00329$** (3 s.f.)**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: `\left(\dfrac{9}{11}\right)^{20}\left(\dfrac{2}{11}\right)`, or `\left(1 - p\right)^{20}p` with 0 < p < 1.
> 
> **A1**: 0.00329, or answers which round to 0.00329.

parts.problemMd:
Guglielma rolls the die 20 times.

Find the probability that

(i) the die lands on a 5 exactly 4 times,

(ii) the die lands on a 5 exactly 4 times, but the final 5 does not occur on the 20th roll.
parts.solutionMd:
(i)

The 20 rolls are independent, each with the same probability $\frac{2}{11}$ of a 5, so $Y$, the number of 5s, follows a binomial distribution

`Y \sim \text{B}\left(20, \; \dfrac{2}{11}\right)`

Use `\text{P}(Y = r) = {}^{n}C_{r} \, p^{r}\left(1 - p\right)^{n - r}` with $r = 4$

`\text{P}(Y = 4) = {}^{20}C_{4}\left(\dfrac{2}{11}\right)^{4}\left(\dfrac{9}{11}\right)^{16}`

**[M1]**

$\text{P} ( Y = 4 ) = 0 . 213520 \dots$

**Final answer:** $\text{P} ( Y = 4 ) = 0 . 214$** (3 s.f.)**

**[A1]**

(ii)

The final 5 is not on the 20th roll, so all four 5s come in the first 19 rolls and the 20th roll is not a 5

$\text{P} = \text{P} ( \text{four 5s in the first 19 rolls} ) \times \text{P} ( \text{20th roll is not a 5} )$

**[M1]**

The first factor is a binomial term with $n = 19$

`\text{P} = {}^{19}C_{4}\left(\dfrac{2}{11}\right)^{4}\left(\dfrac{9}{11}\right)^{15} \times \dfrac{9}{11}`

**[M1]**

$\text{P} = 0 . 170816 \dots$

**Final answer:** $\text{P} = 0 . 171$** (3 s.f.)**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: `{}^{20}C_{4}\left(\dfrac{2}{11}\right)^{4}\left(\dfrac{9}{11}\right)^{16}`.
> 
> **A1**: 0.214, or answers which round to 0.214.
> 
> **M1**: Recognising that all four 5s are in the first 19 rolls and the 20th roll is not a 5.
> 
> **M1**: `{}^{19}C_{4}\left(\dfrac{2}{11}\right)^{4}\left(\dfrac{9}{11}\right)^{15} \times \dfrac{9}{11}`, or equivalently `{}^{19}C_{4}\left(\dfrac{2}{11}\right)^{4}\left(\dfrac{9}{11}\right)^{16}`.
> 
> **A1**: 0.171, or answers which round to 0.171.
> 
> Alternative method: $\frac{16}{20}$ × the answer to (i) scores full marks for (ii).

parts.problemMd:
Bars of a particular brand of chocolate are labelled as weighing 300 g. The probability that a randomly chosen bar weighs between 297 g and 303 g is 0.9596. For bars outside this range, the probability that a bar weighs less than 297 g is equal to the probability that it weighs more than 303 g.

Millie buys 25 of these bars, which may be regarded as a random sample. The random variable $U$ is the number of these bars that weigh less than 297 g.

State the distribution of $U$, giving the values of its parameters.
parts.solutionMd:
The probability outside the range is split equally between the two tails

$\text{P} ( \text{bar weighs less than 297 g} ) = \frac{1-0.9596}{2} = 0 . 0202$

**[B1]**

The 25 bars are a random sample, so they are independent, each with the same probability 0.0202 of weighing less than 297 g

`U \sim \text{B}(25, \; 0.0202)`

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: The probability 0.0202, seen or implied.
> 
> **B1**: B(25, 0.0202), or "binomial with n = 25 and p = 0.0202". Follow through your value of p.

parts.problemMd:
Millie plans to hand out the bars at a meeting attended by 24 people. Bars weighing less than 297 g cannot be handed out.

Find the probability that there will be enough bars to hand out to

(i) all 24 people,

(ii) all but one of the 24 people, but not all of them.
parts.solutionMd:
(i)

24 of the 25 bars are needed, so there is enough for everyone when at most 1 bar is underweight

`\text{P}(U \leq 1) = \left(0.9798\right)^{25} + {}^{25}C_{1}(0.0202)\left(0.9798\right)^{24}`

**[M1]**

$\text{P} ( U \leq 1 ) = 0 . 909842 \dots$

**Final answer:** $\text{P} ( U \leq 1 ) = 0 . 910$** (3 s.f.)**

**[A1]**

(ii)

Enough for exactly 23 people means exactly 2 bars are underweight

`\text{P}(U = 2) = {}^{25}C_{2}\left(0.0202\right)^{2}\left(0.9798\right)^{23}`

$\text{P} ( U = 2 ) = 0 . 0765570 \dots$

**Final answer:** $\text{P} ( U = 2 ) = 0 . 0766$** (3 s.f.)**

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: P(0) + P(1), with both terms correct for their p. Accept unsimplified.
> 
> **A1**: 0.910, or answers which round to 0.910.
> 
> **B1**: 0.0766, or answers which round to 0.0766.
> 
> If 0.910 is given with no working, for example straight from a calculator, award 1 mark only.

parts.problemMd:
Two fair six-sided dice are rolled and the numbers showing are added together. This is done 18 times. The random variable $X$ is the number of times the sum is not equal to 7 or 11.

(i) State the distribution of $X$, giving the values of its parameters.

(ii) State, in context, two assumptions needed for $X$ to be modelled by this distribution.
parts.solutionMd:
(i)

Of the 36 equally likely outcomes, six give a sum of 7 and two give a sum of 11

$\text{P} ( \text{sum is 7 or 11} ) = \frac{6+2}{36} = \frac{8}{36}$

Subtract from 1 to find the probability that the sum is not 7 or 11

$p = 1 - \frac{8}{36} = \frac{28}{36} = \frac{7}{9}$

`X \sim \text{B}\left(18, \; \dfrac{7}{9}\right)`

**[B1]**

(ii)

A binomial model needs a constant probability of success and independent trials

**Final answer:** **The probability that the sum is not 7 or 11 is the same each time the dice are rolled**

**[B1]**

**Final answer:** **The result of each roll of the two dice is independent of the results of the other rolls**

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: B(18, 7/9), or "binomial with n = 18 and p = 7/9". Accept p = 0.778.
> 
> **B1**: The probability is constant for each roll of the two dice, in context.
> 
> **B1**: The rolls are independent of each other, in context.
> 
> The two assumptions are marked independently. "A fixed number of trials" or "two outcomes" are already given in the question, so they do not score.

parts.problemMd: Find the probability that the sum is not equal to 7 or 11 on exactly 14 of the 18 occasions.
parts.solutionMd:
Use `\text{P}(X = r) = {}^{n}C_{r} \, p^{r}\left(1 - p\right)^{n - r}` with $n = 18$, $p = \frac{7}{9}$ and $r = 14$

`\text{P}(X = 14) = {}^{18}C_{14}\left(\dfrac{7}{9}\right)^{14}\left(\dfrac{2}{9}\right)^{4}`

**[M1]**

$\text{P} ( X = 14 ) = 0 . 221232 \dots$

**Final answer:** $\text{P} ( X = 14 ) = 0 . 221$** (3 s.f.)**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: `{}^{18}C_{14}\,p^{14}\left(1 - p\right)^{4}` with your value of p from (a), or 3060 × (7/9)¹⁴ × (2/9)⁴.
> 
> **A1**: 0.221, or answers which round to 0.221.

parts.problemMd:
In a certain region, the probability that any given female mosquito carries the malaria parasite is 0.8.

State, in context, two assumptions needed for the number of female mosquitoes carrying the parasite, in a sample of $n$ female mosquitoes, to be modelled by a binomial distribution.
parts.solutionMd:
A binomial model needs a constant probability of success and independent trials

**Final answer:** **The probability that a female mosquito carries the parasite is 0.8 for every female mosquito in the sample**

**[B1]**

**Final answer:** **Whether one female mosquito carries the parasite is independent of whether any other one does**

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: The probability of a female mosquito carrying the parasite is constant (0.8), in context.
> 
> **B1**: Female mosquitoes carry the parasite independently of each other, in context.
> 
> The two assumptions are marked independently. "A fixed number of trials" or "two outcomes" do not score.

parts.problemMd:
Male mosquitoes cannot transmit the malaria parasite to a human. A female mosquito can transmit the parasite to a human only if she carries it. In this region, 50% of the mosquitoes are male.

Find the probability that, in a random sample of six mosquitoes, none of them is able to transmit the parasite to a human. Give your answer as an exact value.
parts.solutionMd:
A mosquito can transmit the parasite only if it is female and carries the parasite

`\text{P}(\text{can transmit}) = \text{P}(\text{female}) \times \text{P}(\text{carries parasite} \mid \text{female}) = 0.5 \times 0.8`

**[M1]**

$\text{P} ( \text{can transmit} ) = 0 . 4$

**[A1]**

Subtract from 1 for the probability that one mosquito cannot transmit

$\text{P} ( \text{cannot transmit} ) = 1 - 0 . 4 = 0 . 6 = \frac{3}{5}$

**[M1]**

The six mosquitoes are independent, so the number that can transmit has distribution $\text{B} ( 6 ,  0 . 4 )$, and none can transmit with probability

`\text{P}(\text{none of the six can transmit}) = \left(\dfrac{3}{5}\right)^{6}`

**[M1]**

$\text{P} ( \text{none of the six can transmit} ) = \frac{729}{15625}$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: P(can transmit) = 0.5 × 0.8.
> 
> **A1**: 0.4.
> 
> **M1**: P(cannot transmit) = 0.6, or 0.5 + 0.5 × 0.2.
> 
> **M1**: `\left(0.6\right)^{6}`, using your value for one mosquito.
> 
> **A1**: $\frac{729}{15625}$, or the exact decimal 0.046656.
> 
> Alternative method: summing, over the number of females n = 0 to 6, the probability of n females with none of them carrying the parasite, `{}^{6}C_{n}\left(0.5\right)^{6}\left(0.2\right)^{n}`, scores full marks if all seven terms are present and correctly evaluated.

parts.problemMd:
Zara is a gymnast. The probability that she makes a mistake in any given routine is 0.2, independently of other routines. Zara performs 10 routines in a competition. The random variable $X$ is the number of these routines in which Zara makes a mistake.

Find

(i) $\text{E} ( X )$,

(ii) the standard deviation of $X$.
parts.solutionMd:
(i)

The 10 routines are independent, each with the same probability 0.2 of a mistake, so $X$ follows a binomial distribution

`X \sim \text{B}(10, \; 0.2)`

Use $\text{E} ( X ) = n p$

$\text{E} ( X ) = 10 \times 0 . 2$

$\text{E} ( X ) = 2$

**[B1]**

(ii)

Use $\text{Var} ( X ) = n p ( 1 - p )$, then take the square root

$\text{Var} ( X ) = 10 \times 0 . 2 \times 0 . 8 = 1 . 6$

**[M1]**

$\text{standard deviation} = \sqrt{1.6} = 1 . 26491 \dots$

**Final answer:** $\text{standard deviation} = 1 . 26$** (3 s.f.)**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: E(X) = 2.
> 
> **M1**: Var(X) = 10 × 0.2 × 0.8 = 1.6, seen or implied.
> 
> **A1**: 1.26, or answers which round to 1.26. Accept $\sqrt{1.6}$.

parts.problemMd:
Find the probability that Zara makes a mistake in

(i) none of her routines,

(ii) exactly two of her routines,

(iii) no more than two of her routines.
parts.solutionMd:
(i)

None means no mistake in all 10 routines, each with probability 0.8

`\text{P}(X = 0) = \left(0.8\right)^{10}`

**[M1]**

$\text{P} ( X = 0 ) = 0 . 107374 \dots$

**Final answer:** $\text{P} ( X = 0 ) = 0 . 107$** (3 s.f.)**

**[A1]**

(ii)

Use `\text{P}(X = r) = {}^{n}C_{r} \, p^{r}\left(1 - p\right)^{n - r}` with $r = 2$

`\text{P}(X = 2) = {}^{10}C_{2}\left(0.2\right)^{2}\left(0.8\right)^{8}`

**[M1]**

$\text{P} ( X = 2 ) = 0 . 301989 \dots$

**Final answer:** $\text{P} ( X = 2 ) = 0 . 302$** (3 s.f.)**

**[A1]**

(iii)

No more than two means $X = 0$, 1 or 2, so add those three terms

`\text{P}(X \leq 2) = \left(0.8\right)^{10} + {}^{10}C_{1}(0.2)\left(0.8\right)^{9} + {}^{10}C_{2}\left(0.2\right)^{2}\left(0.8\right)^{8}`

**[M1]**

$\text{P} ( X \leq 2 ) = 0 . 107374 \dots + 0 . 268435 \dots + 0 . 301989 \dots = 0 . 677799 \dots$

**Final answer:** $\text{P} ( X \leq 2 ) = 0 . 678$** (3 s.f.)**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: `\left(0.8\right)^{10}`.
> 
> **A1**: 0.107, or answers which round to 0.107.
> 
> **M1**: `{}^{10}C_{2}\left(0.2\right)^{2}\left(0.8\right)^{8}`.
> 
> **A1**: 0.302, or answers which round to 0.302.
> 
> **M1**: P(0) + P(1) + P(2), with all three terms correct. Accept unsimplified.
> 
> **A1**: 0.678, or answers which round to 0.678.
> 
> If 0.107, 0.302 or 0.678 is given with no working, for example straight from a calculator, award 1 mark only for that answer.

parts.problemMd: Given that Zara makes a mistake in at least 2 of her routines, find the probability that she makes a mistake in exactly 3 of her routines.
parts.solutionMd:
Use the definition of conditional probability

`\text{P}(X = 3 \mid X \geq 2) = \dfrac{\text{P}(X = 3 \cap X \geq 2)}{\text{P}(X \geq 2)}`

$X = 3$ already satisfies $X \geq 2$, so the numerator is $\text{P} ( X = 3 )$

`\text{P}(X = 3) = {}^{10}C_{3}\left(0.2\right)^{3}\left(0.8\right)^{7} = 0.201326\ldots`

**[M1]**

The denominator is every outcome except $X = 0$ and $X = 1$

`\text{P}(X \geq 2) = 1 - \left[\left(0.8\right)^{10} + {}^{10}C_{1}(0.2)\left(0.8\right)^{9}\right] = 0.624190\ldots`

**[M1]**

`\text{P}(X = 3 \mid X \geq 2) = \dfrac{0.201326\ldots}{0.624190\ldots} = 0.322540\ldots`

**Final answer:** `\text{P}(X = 3 \mid X \geq 2) = 0.323`** (3 s.f.)**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: P(X = 3) = `{}^{10}C_{3}\left(0.2\right)^{3}\left(0.8\right)^{7}`, seen as the numerator of a fraction.
> 
> **M1**: P(X ≥ 2) = 1 − [P(0) + P(1)], seen as the denominator of a fraction.
> 
> **A1**: 0.323, or answers which round to 0.323.

parts.problemMd: Find the probability that $X$ is less than one standard deviation away from the mean.
parts.solutionMd:
Use the mean and standard deviation from part (a)

$2 - \sqrt{1.6} < X < 2 + \sqrt{1.6}$

$0 . 735 \dots < X < 3 . 26 \dots$

$X$ is a whole number, so this means $X = 1 ,  2 \text{or} 3$

**[M1]**

`\text{P}(1 \leq X \leq 3) = {}^{10}C_{1}(0.2)\left(0.8\right)^{9} + {}^{10}C_{2}\left(0.2\right)^{2}\left(0.8\right)^{8} + {}^{10}C_{3}\left(0.2\right)^{3}\left(0.8\right)^{7}`

**[M1]**

$\text{P} ( 1 \leq X \leq 3 ) = 0 . 771751 \dots$

**Final answer:** $\text{P} ( 1 \leq X \leq 3 ) = 0 . 772$** (3 s.f.)**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Identifying X = 1, 2, 3 from 2 ± 1.26.
> 
> **M1**: P(1) + P(2) + P(3), with all three terms correct. Accept unsimplified.
> 
> **A1**: 0.772, or answers which round to 0.772.

parts.problemMd:
David stands outside a library and asks people who walk past him to answer some market research questions. The probability that a person stops is 0.05, independently of other people.

Find the expected number of people who walk past without stopping before someone stops.
parts.solutionMd:
The people are independent, each with the same probability 0.05 of stopping, so $X$, the number of people who walk past up to and including the first person to stop, follows a geometric distribution

`X \sim \text{Geo}(0.05)`

Use $\text{E} ( X ) = \frac{1}{p}$

$\text{E} ( X ) = \frac{1}{0.05} = 20$

$X$ includes the person who stops, so subtract 1 for the number who walk past without stopping

$20 - 1 = 19$

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: 19.

parts.problemMd:
Find the probability that

(i) the first 20 people walk past David without stopping,

(ii) at least one of the first 100 people who walk past stops.
parts.solutionMd:
(i)

Each of the first 20 people does not stop, with probability 0.95 each

`\text{P}(X > 20) = \left(0.95\right)^{20} = 0.358485\ldots`

**Final answer:** $\text{P} ( X > 20 ) = 0 . 358$** (3 s.f.)**

**[B1]**

(ii)

The only way to fail is for none of the first 100 people to stop, so subtract that from 1

`\text{P}(X \leq 100) = 1 - \left(0.95\right)^{100}`

**[M1]**

$\text{P} ( X \leq 100 ) = 1 - 0 . 00592052 \dots = 0 . 994079 \dots$

**Final answer:** $\text{P} ( X \leq 100 ) = 0 . 994$** (3 s.f.)**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: 0.358, or answers which round to 0.358.
> 
> **M1**: `1 - \left(0.95\right)^{100}`. Accept `1 - \left(0.95\right)^{99}` or `1 - \left(0.95\right)^{101}` for this mark only.
> 
> **A1**: 0.994, or answers which round to 0.994.

parts.problemMd: Given that the first 20 people walk past without stopping, find the probability that at least one of the first 100 people who walk past stops.
parts.solutionMd:
The first 20 people are known not to have stopped, and each person decides independently, so at least one of people 21 to 100 must stop. That is 80 people

`\text{P}(\text{at least one of the next 80 stops}) = 1 - \left(0.95\right)^{80}`

**[M1]**

`1 - \left(0.95\right)^{80} = 1 - 0.0165153\ldots = 0.983484\ldots`

**Final answer:** $\text{Probability} = 0 . 983$** (3 s.f.)**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: `1 - \left(0.95\right)^{80}`, or the conditional-probability ratio `\dfrac{\left(0.95\right)^{20} - \left(0.95\right)^{100}}{\left(0.95\right)^{20}}`.
> 
> **A1**: 0.983, or answers which round to 0.983.

parts.problemMd: Find the probability that the 10th person and the 20th person to walk past are the first two people to stop.
parts.solutionMd:
People 1 to 9 do not stop, person 10 stops, people 11 to 19 do not stop and person 20 stops. These 20 outcomes are independent, so multiply

`\text{P} = \left(0.95\right)^{9}(0.05) \times \left(0.95\right)^{9}(0.05) = \left(0.95\right)^{18}\left(0.05\right)^{2}`

**[M1]**

$\text{P} = 0 . 000993035 \dots$

**Final answer:** $\text{P} = 0 . 000993$** (3 s.f.)**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: `\left(0.95\right)^{18}\left(0.05\right)^{2}`, or the product of two terms `\left(0.95\right)^{9}(0.05)`.
> 
> **A1**: 0.000993, or answers which round to 0.000993. Accept 9.93 × 10⁻⁴.

parts.problemMd: Find the least number of people who must walk past so that the probability that at least one of them stops is at least 0.999.
parts.solutionMd:
For $n$ people, at least one stops unless none of them does

`1 - \left(0.95\right)^{n} \geq 0.999`

**[M1]**

Rearrange

`\left(0.95\right)^{n} \leq 0.001`

Take logarithms of both sides. $\text{ln}  0 . 95$ is negative, so dividing by it reverses the inequality

$n  \text{ln}  0 . 95 \leq \text{ln}  0 . 001$

$n \geq \frac{\text{ln}0.001}{\text{ln}0.95} = 134 . 67 \dots$

**[M1]**

$n$ must be a whole number

$n = 135$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: `1 - \left(0.95\right)^{n} \geq 0.999`, or `\left(0.95\right)^{n} \leq 0.001`. Allow "=" throughout.
> 
> **M1**: Taking logarithms of both sides, or evaluating `1 - \left(0.95\right)^{n}` for both n = 134 (0.99896…) and n = 135 (0.99902…).
> 
> **A1**: n = 135 only, as a single integer.

parts.problemMd:
Anand and Beatrix each throw a dart at a target repeatedly until they hit it for the first time. On each throw, the probability that the thrower hits the target is $p$, independently of all other throws by either of them.

(i) Show that the probability that Anand and Beatrix make a total of 4 throws between them can be written as `kp^{2}\left(1 - p\right)^{2}`, where $k$ is a constant to be found.

(ii) Given that the probability that they make a total of 4 throws is 0.1875, find the value of $p$.
parts.solutionMd:
(i)

Each person needs at least one throw, so list the ways to split a total of 4 throws as (Anand, Beatrix)

*(1, 3), (2, 2) or (3, 1)*

**[M1]**

Use `\text{P}(\text{first hit on throw } r) = p\left(1 - p\right)^{r - 1}` for each person and multiply, since they are independent

`(1, \; 3): \; p \times p\left(1 - p\right)^{2} = p^{2}\left(1 - p\right)^{2}`

`(2, \; 2): \; p(1 - p) \times p(1 - p) = p^{2}\left(1 - p\right)^{2}`

`(3, \; 1): \; p\left(1 - p\right)^{2} \times p = p^{2}\left(1 - p\right)^{2}`

**[M1]**

Add the three cases

`\text{P}(\text{total of 4 throws}) = 3p^{2}\left(1 - p\right)^{2}`

$k = 3$

**[A1]**

(ii)

Set the result from (i) equal to 0.1875

`3p^{2}\left(1 - p\right)^{2} = 0.1875`

Divide by 3

`\left[p(1 - p)\right]^{2} = 0.0625`

**[M1]**

Take the square root. $p$ and $1 - p$ are both probabilities, so $p ( 1 - p )$ cannot be negative

$p ( 1 - p ) = 0 . 25$

Rearrange and factorise

$p^{2} - p + 0 . 25 = 0$

`\left(p - 0.5\right)^{2} = 0`

$p = 0 . 5$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Identifying the three cases (1, 3), (2, 2) and (3, 1), and no others.
> 
> **M1**: A correct product of two geometric probabilities for at least one case, e.g. `p \times p\left(1 - p\right)^{2}`.
> 
> **A1**: `3p^{2}\left(1 - p\right)^{2}` with k = 3 stated. All three cases must be shown, as the form is given.
> 
> **M1**: `3p^{2}\left(1 - p\right)^{2} = 0.1875`, simplified to an equation in $p ( 1 - p )$, or expanded to a quartic.
> 
> **A1**: p = 0.5 only. A negative value of $p ( 1 - p )$ must be rejected, or not given.

parts.problemMd:
The probability that Chen wins a game of chess against a computer is 0.2, independently of other games. Chen plays $n$ games. The random variable $Y$ is the number of these games that Chen wins.

Find the largest value of $n$ for which the probability that Chen wins at least one game is less than 0.9.
parts.solutionMd:
The $n$ games are independent, each with the same probability 0.2 of a win, so $Y$ follows a binomial distribution

`Y \sim \text{B}(n, \; 0.2)`

Chen wins at least one game unless he loses all $n$, each with probability 0.8

`\text{P}(Y \geq 1) = 1 - \left(0.8\right)^{n} < 0.9`

**[M1]**

Rearrange

`\left(0.8\right)^{n} > 0.1`

Take logarithms of both sides. $\text{ln}  0 . 8$ is negative, so dividing by it reverses the inequality

$n  \text{ln}  0 . 8 > \text{ln}  0 . 1$

$n < \frac{\text{ln}0.1}{\text{ln}0.8} = 10 . 318 \dots$

**[M1]**

$n$ must be a whole number

$n = 10$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: `1 - \left(0.8\right)^{n} < 0.9`, or `\left(0.8\right)^{n} > 0.1`. Allow "=" throughout.
> 
> **M1**: Taking logarithms of both sides, or evaluating `1 - \left(0.8\right)^{n}` for both n = 10 (0.8926…) and n = 11 (0.9141…).
> 
> **A1**: n = 10 only, as a single integer.

parts.problemMd:
Maifreda rolls a biased die with faces numbered 1 to 6. The probability that the die lands on a prime number is $\frac{1}{2}$ and the probability that it lands on a square number is $\frac{5}{16}$.

Find the expected number of rolls needed to obtain a 6 for the first time.
parts.solutionMd:
The primes on the die are 2, 3 and 5, and the squares are 1 and 4. That leaves only the 6, so subtract from 1

$\text{P} ( 6 ) = 1 - \frac{1}{2} - \frac{5}{16} = \frac{3}{16}$

**[M1]**

The rolls are independent, each with the same probability $\frac{3}{16}$ of a 6, so the number of rolls up to and including the first 6 is `X \sim \text{Geo}\left(\dfrac{3}{16}\right)`. Use $\text{E} ( X ) = \frac{1}{p}$

$\text{E} ( X ) = \frac{1}{\frac{3}{16}}$

$\text{E} ( X ) = \frac{16}{3}$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: P(6) = 1 − 1/2 − 5/16 = 3/16.
> 
> **A1**: $\frac{16}{3}$, or answers which round to 5.33. Not 1/(3/16) left unevaluated.

parts.problemMd:
Maifreda rolls the die 20 times.

Find the probability that

(i) the die lands on a 6 exactly four times,

(ii) the die lands on a 6 exactly four times, and all four 6s occur within the first $k$ rolls, where $4 \leq k \leq 20$. Give your answer in terms of $k$.
parts.solutionMd:
(i)

The 20 rolls are independent, each with the same probability $\frac{3}{16}$ of a 6, so $Y$, the number of 6s, follows a binomial distribution

`Y \sim \text{B}\left(20, \; \dfrac{3}{16}\right)`

Use `\text{P}(Y = r) = {}^{n}C_{r} \, p^{r}\left(1 - p\right)^{n - r}` with $r = 4$

`\text{P}(Y = 4) = {}^{20}C_{4}\left(\dfrac{3}{16}\right)^{4}\left(\dfrac{13}{16}\right)^{16}`

**[M1]**

$\text{P} ( Y = 4 ) = 0 . 216009 \dots$

**Final answer:** $\text{P} ( Y = 4 ) = 0 . 216$** (3 s.f.)**

**[A1]**

(ii)

All four 6s are in the first $k$ rolls, and none of the remaining $20 - k$ rolls is a 6

$\text{P} = \text{P} ( \text{four 6s in the first} k \text{rolls} ) \times \text{P} ( \text{no 6s in the last} 20 - k \text{rolls} )$

**[M1]**

The first factor is a binomial term with $n = k$

`\text{P} = {}^{k}C_{4}\left(\dfrac{3}{16}\right)^{4}\left(\dfrac{13}{16}\right)^{k - 4} \times \left(\dfrac{13}{16}\right)^{20 - k}`

**[M1]**

Add the powers of $\frac{13}{16}$, since $( k - 4 ) + ( 20 - k ) = 16$

`\text{P} = {}^{k}C_{4}\left(\dfrac{3}{16}\right)^{4}\left(\dfrac{13}{16}\right)^{16}`

**[A1 A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: `{}^{20}C_{4}\left(\dfrac{3}{16}\right)^{4}\left(\dfrac{13}{16}\right)^{16}`, using your p from (a).
> 
> **A1**: 0.216, or answers which round to 0.216.
> 
> **M1**: Recognising four 6s in the first k rolls and no 6s in the remaining 20 − k rolls.
> 
> **M1**: `{}^{k}C_{4}\,p^{4}\left(1 - p\right)^{k - 4} \times \left(1 - p\right)^{20 - k}`, unsimplified.
> 
> **A1**: The powers of $\frac{13}{16}$ combined correctly to 16.
> 
> **A1**: `{}^{k}C_{4}\left(\dfrac{3}{16}\right)^{4}\left(\dfrac{13}{16}\right)^{16}`, fully correct. Accept the equivalent `\dfrac{{}^{k}C_{4}}{{}^{20}C_{4}}` × the answer to (i).

parts.problemMd:
The random variable $Z$ has the standard normal distribution.

Find

(i) $\text{P} ( Z > 0 . 74 )$

(ii) $\text{P} ( Z > - 0 . 74 )$

(iii) $\text{P} ( Z > 2 . 142 )$

(iv) $\text{P} ( Z > - 1 . 516 )$
parts.solutionMd:
(i)

The table gives areas to the left, so the area to the right of 0.74 is 1 minus the area to its left

![Standard normal curve with the area to the left of 0.74 labelled Φ(0.74) and the shaded area to the right of 0.74 labelled 1 − Φ(0.74)](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-probability-and-statistics-1/statistical-distributions/normal-distribution/assets/053-standard-normal-curve-with-the-area-to-the-left-.png)

$\text{P} ( Z > 0 . 74 ) = 1 - Φ ( 0 . 74 )$

In the table of the normal distribution function in the formula booklet, the 0.7 row and the 4 column give

$Φ ( 0 . 74 ) = 0 . 7704$

$\text{P} ( Z > 0 . 74 ) = 1 - 0 . 7704$

$\text{P} ( Z > 0 . 74 ) = 0 . 2296$

**[B1]**

(ii)

The curve is symmetrical about 0, so the area to the right of −0.74 equals the area to the left of 0.74

![Two standard normal curves side by side: the first has the area to the right of −0.74 shaded, the second has the equal area to the left of 0.74 shaded, labelled Φ(0.74)](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-probability-and-statistics-1/statistical-distributions/normal-distribution/assets/054-two-standard-normal-curves-side-by-side-the-firs.png)

$\text{P} ( Z > - 0 . 74 ) = Φ ( 0 . 74 )$

Using the value of $Φ ( 0 . 74 )$ from (i)

$\text{P} ( Z > - 0 . 74 ) = 0 . 7704$

**[B1]**

(iii)

As in part (i), subtract the area to the left of 2.142 from 1. In the 2.1 row, the 4 column gives 0.9838 and ADD 2 gives 1

$\text{P} ( Z > 2 . 142 ) = 1 - Φ ( 2 . 142 )$

$\text{P} ( Z > 2 . 142 ) = 1 - 0 . 9839$

$\text{P} ( Z > 2 . 142 ) = 0 . 0161$

**[B1]**

(iv)

As in part (ii), use symmetry. In the 1.5 row, the 1 column gives 0.9345 and ADD 6 gives 7

$\text{P} ( Z > - 1 . 516 ) = Φ ( 1 . 516 )$

$\text{P} ( Z > - 1 . 516 ) = 0 . 9345 + 0 . 0007$

$\text{P} ( Z > - 1 . 516 ) = 0 . 9352$

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: P(Z > 0.74) = 0.2296.
> 
> **B1**: P(Z > −0.74) = 0.7704.
> 
> **B1**: P(Z > 2.142) = 0.0161.
> 
> **B1**: P(Z > −1.516) = 0.9352. Accept 0.9353 from a calculator.
> 
> The four answers are marked independently.

> **B1**: z = −1.598. Accept −1.599 from a calculator.
> 
> **B1**: z = −3.291.
> 
> The four answers are marked independently. A positive value of z does not score.

parts.problemMd:
The random variable $Z$ has the standard normal distribution.

Find

(i) $\text{P} ( 0 . 12 < Z < 1 . 34 )$

(ii) $\text{P} ( 1 . 037 < Z < 2 . 913 )$

(iii) $\text{P} ( - 2 < Z < 1 )$

(iv) $\text{P} ( - 1 . 5 < Z < - 0 . 5 )$
parts.solutionMd:
(i)

The area between two values is the area to the left of the upper value minus the area to the left of the lower value

![Standard normal curve with the area between 0.12 and 1.34 shaded and labelled Φ(1.34) − Φ(0.12)](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-probability-and-statistics-1/statistical-distributions/normal-distribution/assets/066-standard-normal-curve-with-the-area-between-0-12.png)

$\text{P} ( a < Z < b ) = Φ ( b ) - Φ ( a )$

$\text{P} ( 0 . 12 < Z < 1 . 34 ) = Φ ( 1 . 34 ) - Φ ( 0 . 12 )$

In the table of the normal distribution function in the formula booklet, the 1.3 row and the 4 column give

$Φ ( 1 . 34 ) = 0 . 9099$

The 0.1 row and the 2 column give

$Φ ( 0 . 12 ) = 0 . 5478$

$\text{P} ( 0 . 12 < Z < 1 . 34 ) = 0 . 9099 - 0 . 5478 = 0 . 3621$

**Final answer:** $\text{P} ( 0 . 12 < Z < 1 . 34 ) = 0 . 362$** (3 s.f.)**

**[B1]**

(ii)

In the same table, the 1.0 row and the 3 column give 0.8485. For the third decimal place, ADD 7 in the 1.0 row is 16, so add 0.0016

$Φ ( 1 . 037 ) = 0 . 8485 + 0 . 0016 = 0 . 8501$

The 2.9 row and the 1 column give 0.9982, and ADD 3 in the 2.9 row is 0

$Φ ( 2 . 913 ) = 0 . 9982 + 0 = 0 . 9982$

$\text{P} ( 1 . 037 < Z < 2 . 913 ) = Φ ( 2 . 913 ) - Φ ( 1 . 037 )$

$\text{P} ( 1 . 037 < Z < 2 . 913 ) = 0 . 9982 - 0 . 8501 = 0 . 1481$

**Final answer:** $\text{P} ( 1 . 037 < Z < 2 . 913 ) = 0 . 148$** (3 s.f.)**

**[B1]**

(iii)

The lower value is negative, so use $Φ ( - 2 ) = 1 - Φ ( 2 )$

$\text{P} ( - 2 < Z < 1 ) = Φ ( 1 ) - Φ ( - 2 )$

`\text{P}(-2 < Z < 1) = \mathrm{\Phi}(1) - \left(1 - \mathrm{\Phi}(2)\right)`

In the same table, the 1.0 row and the 0 column give

$Φ ( 1 ) = 0 . 8413$

The 2.0 row and the 0 column give

$Φ ( 2 ) = 0 . 9772$

$\text{P} ( - 2 < Z < 1 ) = 0 . 8413 - ( 1 - 0 . 9772 ) = 0 . 8185$

**Final answer:** $\text{P} ( - 2 < Z < 1 ) = 0 . 819$** (3 s.f.)**

**[B1]**

(iv)

By symmetry, the area between −1.5 and −0.5 equals the area between 0.5 and 1.5

![Two standard normal curves side by side: the first has the area between −1.5 and −0.5 shaded, the second has the equal area between 0.5 and 1.5 shaded](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-probability-and-statistics-1/statistical-distributions/normal-distribution/assets/067-two-standard-normal-curves-side-by-side-the-firs.png)

$\text{P} ( - 1 . 5 < Z < - 0 . 5 ) = Φ ( 1 . 5 ) - Φ ( 0 . 5 )$

In the same table, the 1.5 row and the 0 column give

$Φ ( 1 . 5 ) = 0 . 9332$

The 0.5 row and the 0 column give

$Φ ( 0 . 5 ) = 0 . 6915$

$\text{P} ( - 1 . 5 < Z < - 0 . 5 ) = 0 . 9332 - 0 . 6915 = 0 . 2417$

**Final answer:** $\text{P} ( - 1 . 5 < Z < - 0 . 5 ) = 0 . 242$** (3 s.f.)**

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: P(0.12 < Z < 1.34) = 0.362, or answers which round to 0.362.
> 
> **B1**: P(1.037 < Z < 2.913) = 0.148, or answers which round to 0.148.
> 
> **B1**: P(−2 < Z < 1) = 0.819, or answers which round to 0.819. Accept 0.8185.
> 
> **B1**: P(−1.5 < Z < −0.5) = 0.242, or answers which round to 0.242.
> 
> The four answers are marked independently.

parts.problemMd:
Find the value of $z$ such that

(i) $\text{P} ( 0 < Z < z ) = 0 . 499$

(ii) $\text{P} ( z < Z < 2 . 093 ) = 0 . 319$

(iii) $\text{P} ( z < Z < 1 . 3 ) = 0 . 9027$

(iv) $\text{P} ( - z < Z < z ) = 0 . 6826$
parts.solutionMd:
(i)

Half the area lies to the left of 0, so $Φ ( 0 ) = 0 . 5$

$Φ ( z ) - Φ ( 0 ) = 0 . 499$

$Φ ( z ) = 0 . 499 + 0 . 5 = 0 . 999$

0.999 is in the table of critical values for the normal distribution in the formula booklet

$z = 3 . 090$

**[B1]**

(ii)

Find $Φ ( 2 . 093 )$ first. In the table of the normal distribution function in the formula booklet, the 2.0 row and the 9 column give 0.9817, and ADD 3 in the 2.0 row is 1, so add 0.0001

$Φ ( 2 . 093 ) = 0 . 9817 + 0 . 0001 = 0 . 9818$

$Φ ( 2 . 093 ) - Φ ( z ) = 0 . 319$

$Φ ( z ) = 0 . 9818 - 0 . 319 = 0 . 6628$

0.6628 is in the 0.4 row and the 2 column

$z = 0 . 42$

**[B1]**

(iii)

In the table of the normal distribution function in the formula booklet, the 1.3 row and the 0 column give

$Φ ( 1 . 3 ) = 0 . 9032$

$Φ ( 1 . 3 ) - Φ ( z ) = 0 . 9027$

$Φ ( z ) = 0 . 9032 - 0 . 9027 = 0 . 0005$

0.0005 is less than 0.5, so $z$ is negative. By symmetry

$Φ ( - z ) = 1 - 0 . 0005 = 0 . 9995$

0.9995 is in the table of critical values for the normal distribution in the formula booklet

$- z = 3 . 291$

$z = - 3 . 291$

**[B1]**

(iv)

![Standard normal curve with the area 0.6826 between −z and z shaded](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-probability-and-statistics-1/statistical-distributions/normal-distribution/assets/068-standard-normal-curve-with-the-area-0-6826-betwe.png)

The area between $- z$ and $z$ is the area to the left of $z$ minus the area to the left of $- z$

$\text{P} ( - z < Z < z ) = Φ ( z ) - Φ ( - z )$

By symmetry, the area to the left of $- z$ equals the area to the right of $z$

$Φ ( - z ) = 1 - Φ ( z )$

Substitute this into the first line

`\text{P}(-z < Z < z) = \mathrm{\Phi}(z) - \left(1 - \mathrm{\Phi}(z)\right)`

$\text{P} ( - z < Z < z ) = 2 Φ ( z ) - 1$

The area between $- z$ and $z$ is 0.6826

$2 Φ ( z ) - 1 = 0 . 6826$

$Φ ( z ) = \frac{1.6826}{2} = 0 . 8413$

0.8413 is in the 1.0 row and the 0 column

$z = 1$

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: z = 3.090. Accept 3.09.
> 
> **B1**: z = 0.42.
> 
> **B1**: z = −3.291.
> 
> **B1**: z = 1. Accept 1.00.
> 
> The four answers are marked independently.

parts.problemMd:
The times taken, in minutes, to complete a puzzle are normally distributed with mean 21 minutes and standard deviation 4 minutes.

Find the probability that a randomly chosen person takes more than 26 minutes to complete the puzzle.
parts.solutionMd:
Let $X$ be the time taken, in minutes, so `X \sim \text{N}(21, \; 4^{2})`

To use the table, standardise: the value 26 on $X$ matches the value $z = \frac{x-μ}{σ}$ on $Z$

![A normal curve for X with mean 21 and the area to the right of 26 shaded, an arrow, and a standard normal curve with the matching area to the right of 1.25 shaded](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-probability-and-statistics-1/statistical-distributions/normal-distribution/assets/061-a-normal-curve-for-x-with-mean-21-and-the-area-t.png)

`\text{P}(X > 26) = \text{P}\left(Z > \dfrac{26 - 21}{4}\right)`

$\text{P} ( X > 26 ) = \text{P} ( Z > 1 . 25 )$

**[M1]**

The table of the normal distribution function in the formula booklet gives the area to the left of 1.25, so subtract it from 1

![Extract from the normal distribution function table showing the 1.1, 1.2 and 1.3 rows, with the 1.2 row, the 5 column and the value 0.8944 ringed](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-probability-and-statistics-1/statistical-distributions/normal-distribution/assets/062-extract-from-the-normal-distribution-function-ta.png)

$\text{P} ( X > 26 ) = 1 - Φ ( 1 . 25 )$

**[M1]**

The 1.2 row and the 5 column of the table give

$Φ ( 1 . 25 ) = 0 . 8944$

$\text{P} ( X > 26 ) = 1 - 0 . 8944 = 0 . 1056$

**Final answer:** $\text{P} ( X > 26 ) = 0 . 106$** (3 s.f.)**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Standardising with 26, 21 and 4. Dividing by 16, or by the square root of 4, does not score.
> 
> **M1**: 1 − Φ(their z), leading to a probability less than 0.5.
> 
> **A1**: P(X > 26) = 0.106, or answers which round to 0.106. Accept 0.1056.
> 
> If 0.106 is given with no working, for example straight from a calculator, award 1 mark only.

parts.problemMd:
The weights of female leopards in a particular region are normally distributed with mean 54 kg and standard deviation 5 kg.

Find the probability that a randomly chosen female leopard from this region weighs

(i) less than 51 kg,

(ii) at least 58 kg.
parts.solutionMd:
(i)

Let $W$ be the weight, in kg, so `W \sim \text{N}(54, \; 5^{2})`

Standardise using the formula

$Z = \frac{X-μ}{σ}$

Substitute $μ = 54$ and $σ = 5$

`\text{P}(W < 51) = \text{P}\left(Z < \dfrac{51 - 54}{5}\right)`

$\text{P} ( W < 51 ) = \text{P} ( Z < - 0 . 6 )$

**[M1]**

The table only gives positive $z$-values. By symmetry, the area to the left of −0.6 equals the area to the right of 0.6

![Two standard normal curves side by side: the first has the area to the left of −0.6 shaded and labelled Φ(−0.6), the second has the equal area to the right of 0.6 shaded and labelled 1 − Φ(0.6)](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-probability-and-statistics-1/statistical-distributions/normal-distribution/assets/063-two-standard-normal-curves-side-by-side-the-firs.png)

$\text{P} ( W < 51 ) = 1 - Φ ( 0 . 6 )$

**[M1]**

In the table of the normal distribution function in the formula booklet, the 0.6 row and the 0 column give

$Φ ( 0 . 6 ) = 0 . 7257$

$\text{P} ( W < 51 ) = 1 - 0 . 7257 = 0 . 2743$

**Final answer:** $\text{P} ( W < 51 ) = 0 . 274$** (3 s.f.)**

**[A1]**

(ii)

"At least 58 kg" means $W \geq 58$. For a continuous variable, $\text{P} ( W \geq 58 ) = \text{P} ( W > 58 )$

`\text{P}(W \geq 58) = \text{P}\left(Z \geq \dfrac{58 - 54}{5}\right)`

$\text{P} ( W \geq 58 ) = \text{P} ( Z \geq 0 . 8 )$

**[M1]**

![Standard normal curve with the area to the left of 0.8 labelled Φ(0.8) and the shaded area to the right of 0.8 labelled 1 − Φ(0.8)](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-probability-and-statistics-1/statistical-distributions/normal-distribution/assets/064-standard-normal-curve-with-the-area-to-the-left-.png)

$\text{P} ( W \geq 58 ) = 1 - Φ ( 0 . 8 )$

**[M1]**

In the same table, the 0.8 row and the 0 column give

$Φ ( 0 . 8 ) = 0 . 7881$

$\text{P} ( W \geq 58 ) = 1 - 0 . 7881 = 0 . 2119$

**Final answer:** $\text{P} ( W \geq 58 ) = 0 . 212$** (3 s.f.)**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Standardising 51 with 54 and 5. Dividing by 25 does not score.
> 
> **M1**: 1 − Φ(0.6), or Φ(−0.6) correctly found, leading to a probability less than 0.5.
> 
> **A1**: 0.274, or answers which round to 0.274.
> 
> **M1**: Standardising 58 with 54 and 5. No continuity correction: 57.5 or 58.5 does not score.
> 
> **M1**: 1 − Φ(their z), leading to a probability less than 0.5.
> 
> **A1**: 0.212, or answers which round to 0.212.
> 
> If 0.274 or 0.212 is given with no working, for example straight from a calculator, award 1 mark only for that answer.

parts.problemMd:
The heights of adult males in a city are normally distributed with mean 187 cm and standard deviation 10 cm.

Find the probability that a randomly chosen adult male in this city has a height between 190 cm and 203 cm.
parts.solutionMd:
Let $H$ be the height, in cm, so `H \sim \text{N}(187, \; 10^{2})`

Standardise using the formula

$Z = \frac{X-μ}{σ}$

Substitute $μ = 187$ and $σ = 10$ for both values

`\text{P}(190 < H < 203) = \text{P}\left(\dfrac{190 - 187}{10} < Z < \dfrac{203 - 187}{10}\right)`

$\text{P} ( 190 < H < 203 ) = \text{P} ( 0 . 3 < Z < 1 . 6 )$

**[M1]**

The area between the two values is the area to the left of 1.6 minus the area to the left of 0.3

![Standard normal curve with the area between 0.3 and 1.6 shaded and labelled Φ(1.6) − Φ(0.3)](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-probability-and-statistics-1/statistical-distributions/normal-distribution/assets/065-standard-normal-curve-with-the-area-between-0-3-.png)

$\text{P} ( 190 < H < 203 ) = Φ ( 1 . 6 ) - Φ ( 0 . 3 )$

**[M1]**

In the table of the normal distribution function in the formula booklet, the 1.6 row and the 0 column give

$Φ ( 1 . 6 ) = 0 . 9452$

The 0.3 row and the 0 column give

$Φ ( 0 . 3 ) = 0 . 6179$

$\text{P} ( 190 < H < 203 ) = 0 . 9452 - 0 . 6179 = 0 . 3273$

**Final answer:** $\text{P} ( 190 < H < 203 ) = 0 . 327$** (3 s.f.)**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Standardising either 190 or 203 with 187 and 10. Dividing by 100 does not score.
> 
> **M1**: Φ(1.6) − Φ(0.3), from their two z-values, giving a probability.
> 
> **A1**: 0.327, or answers which round to 0.327.
> 
> If 0.327 is given with no working, for example straight from a calculator, award 1 mark only.

parts.problemMd:
The random variable `X \sim \text{N}(32, \; 9)`.

Write down the mean and the standard deviation of $X$.
parts.solutionMd:
`X \sim \text{N}(\mu, \; \sigma^{2})` gives the mean and the variance

$μ = 32$

**[B1]**

The standard deviation is the square root of the variance

$σ = \sqrt{9}$

$σ = 3$

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: Mean = 32.
> 
> **B1**: Standard deviation = 3. A standard deviation of 9 does not score.
> 
> The two answers are marked independently.

parts.problemMd:
Find

(i) $\text{P} ( X \leq 34 )$

(ii) $\text{P} ( X \geq 39 )$

(iii) $\text{P} ( 34 \leq X \leq 39 )$
parts.solutionMd:
(i)

34 is above the mean of 32, so the probability is more than 0.5

![Normal curve with the mean 32 marked by a dashed line and the area to the left of 34 shaded](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-probability-and-statistics-1/statistical-distributions/normal-distribution/assets/045-normal-curve-with-the-mean-32-marked-by-a-dashed.png)

Standardise using the formula

$Z = \frac{X-μ}{σ}$

Substitute $μ = 32$ and $σ = 3$

`\text{P}(X \leq 34) = \text{P}\left(Z \leq \dfrac{34 - 32}{3}\right)`

$\text{P} ( X \leq 34 ) = \text{P} ( Z \leq 0 . 667 ) = Φ ( 0 . 667 )$

**[M1]**

To find $Φ ( 0 . 667 )$, use the table of the normal distribution function in the formula booklet. The 0.6 row and the 6 column give

$Φ ( 0 . 66 ) = 0 . 7454$

For the third decimal place, 7, look in the ADD columns: ADD 7 in the 0.6 row is 23, so add 0.0023

$Φ ( 0 . 667 ) = 0 . 7454 + 0 . 0023 = 0 . 7477$

**Final answer:** $\text{P} ( X \leq 34 ) = 0 . 748$** (3 s.f.)**

**[A1]**

(ii)

![Normal curve with the mean 32 marked by a dashed line and the small area to the right of 39 shaded](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-probability-and-statistics-1/statistical-distributions/normal-distribution/assets/046-normal-curve-with-the-mean-32-marked-by-a-dashed.png)

Standardise 39 in the same way

`\text{P}(X \geq 39) = \text{P}\left(Z \geq \dfrac{39 - 32}{3}\right) = \text{P}(Z \geq 2.333)`

The area to the right is 1 minus the area to the left

$\text{P} ( X \geq 39 ) = 1 - Φ ( 2 . 333 )$

**[M1]**

In the same table, the 2.3 row and the 3 column give

$Φ ( 2 . 33 ) = 0 . 9901$

ADD 3 in the 2.3 row is 1, so add 0.0001

$Φ ( 2 . 333 ) = 0 . 9901 + 0 . 0001 = 0 . 9902$

$\text{P} ( X \geq 39 ) = 1 - 0 . 9902 = 0 . 0098$

**Final answer:** $\text{P} ( X \geq 39 ) = 0 . 00980$** (3 s.f.)**

**[A1]**

(iii)

![Normal curve with the mean 32 marked by a dashed line and the area between 34 and 39 shaded](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-probability-and-statistics-1/statistical-distributions/normal-distribution/assets/047-normal-curve-with-the-mean-32-marked-by-a-dashed.png)

Subtract the area to the left of 34 from the area to the left of 39, using the values of $Φ$ found in (i) and (ii)

$\text{P} ( 34 \leq X \leq 39 ) = Φ ( 2 . 333 ) - Φ ( 0 . 667 )$

**[M1]**

$\text{P} ( 34 \leq X \leq 39 ) = 0 . 9902 - 0 . 7477 = 0 . 2425$

**Final answer:** $\text{P} ( 34 \leq X \leq 39 ) = 0 . 243$** (3 s.f.)**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Standardising 34 with 32 and 3, and using Φ of the result. Dividing by 9 instead of 3 does not score.
> 
> **A1**: P(X ≤ 34) = 0.748, or answers which round to 0.748.
> 
> **M1**: Standardising 39 with 32 and 3, and subtracting Φ of the result from 1.
> 
> **A1**: P(X ≥ 39) = 0.00980, or answers which round to 0.0098. Accept 0.00982.
> 
> **M1**: The difference of the two Φ values, with the larger first.
> 
> **A1**: P(34 ≤ X ≤ 39) = 0.243, or answers which round to 0.243.
> 
> If 0.748, 0.00980 or 0.243 is given with no working, for example straight from a calculator, award 1 mark only for that answer.

parts.problemMd:
The random variable $Z$ has the standard normal distribution.

Find

(i) $\text{P} ( Z < 1 . 5 )$

(ii) $\text{P} ( Z > - 0 . 8 )$

(iii) $\text{P} ( - 2 . 1 < Z < - 0 . 3 )$
parts.solutionMd:
(i)

In the table of the normal distribution function in the formula booklet, the 1.5 row and the 0 column give the area to the left of 1.5

![Standard normal curve with the mean 0 marked by a dashed line and the area to the left of 1.5 shaded](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-probability-and-statistics-1/statistical-distributions/normal-distribution/assets/039-standard-normal-curve-with-the-mean-0-marked-by-.png)

$\text{P} ( Z < 1 . 5 ) = Φ ( 1 . 5 )$

$\text{P} ( Z < 1 . 5 ) = 0 . 9332$

**[B1]**

(ii)

By symmetry, the area to the right of −0.8 equals the area to the left of 0.8

![Two standard normal curves side by side: the first has the area to the right of −0.8 shaded, the second has the equal area to the left of 0.8 shaded](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-probability-and-statistics-1/statistical-distributions/normal-distribution/assets/040-two-standard-normal-curves-side-by-side-the-firs.png)

$\text{P} ( Z > - 0 . 8 ) = Φ ( 0 . 8 )$

In the same table, the 0.8 row and the 0 column give

$\text{P} ( Z > - 0 . 8 ) = 0 . 7881$

**[B1]**

(iii)

By symmetry, the area between −2.1 and −0.3 equals the area between 0.3 and 2.1

![Two standard normal curves side by side: the first has the area between −2.1 and −0.3 shaded, the second has the equal area between 0.3 and 2.1 shaded](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-probability-and-statistics-1/statistical-distributions/normal-distribution/assets/041-two-standard-normal-curves-side-by-side-the-firs.png)

$\text{P} ( - 2 . 1 < Z < - 0 . 3 ) = Φ ( 2 . 1 ) - Φ ( 0 . 3 )$

**[M1]**

In the same table, the 2.1 row and the 0 column give

$Φ ( 2 . 1 ) = 0 . 9821$

The 0.3 row and the 0 column give

$Φ ( 0 . 3 ) = 0 . 6179$

$\text{P} ( - 2 . 1 < Z < - 0 . 3 ) = 0 . 9821 - 0 . 6179$

$\text{P} ( - 2 . 1 < Z < - 0 . 3 ) = 0 . 3642$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: P(Z < 1.5) = 0.9332.
> 
> **B1**: P(Z > −0.8) = 0.7881.
> 
> **M1**: Φ(2.1) − Φ(0.3), or an equivalent such as (1 − Φ(0.3)) − (1 − Φ(2.1)).
> 
> **A1**: P(−2.1 < Z < −0.3) = 0.3642, or answers which round to 0.364.
> 
> The answers to (i), (ii) and (iii) are marked independently.

parts.problemMd:
The random variable $X$ is normally distributed with mean 2 and standard deviation 0.1.

Find the values of $a$, $b$, $c$ and $d$ such that

(i) $\text{P} ( X < a ) = \text{P} ( Z < 1 . 5 )$

(ii) $\text{P} ( X > b ) = \text{P} ( Z > - 0 . 8 )$

(iii) $\text{P} ( c < X < d ) = \text{P} ( - 2 . 1 < Z < - 0 . 3 )$
parts.solutionMd:
Each value of $X$ standardises to the matching value of $Z$, so rearrange the standardisation

$z = \frac{x-μ}{σ}$

$x = μ + z σ = 2 + 0 . 1 z$

(i)

$a = 2 + 0 . 1 \times 1 . 5$

$a = 2 . 15$

**[B1]**

(ii)

$b = 2 + 0 . 1 \times ( - 0 . 8 )$

$b = 1 . 92$

**[B1]**

(iii)

The interval from $c$ to $d$ on $X$ matches the interval from −2.1 to −0.3 on $Z$

![A normal curve for X with mean 2 and the area between c and d shaded, an arrow, and a standard normal curve with the matching area between −2.1 and −0.3 shaded](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-probability-and-statistics-1/statistical-distributions/normal-distribution/assets/042-a-normal-curve-for-x-with-mean-2-and-the-area-be.png)

$c = 2 + 0 . 1 \times ( - 2 . 1 )$

$c = 1 . 79$

**[B1]**

$d = 2 + 0 . 1 \times ( - 0 . 3 )$

$d = 1 . 97$

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: a = 2.15.
> 
> **B1**: b = 1.92.
> 
> **B1**: c = 1.79.
> 
> **B1**: d = 1.97.
> 
> The four values are marked independently.

parts.problemMd:
The random variable `X \sim \text{N}(23, \; 4^{2})`.

Find

(i) $\text{P} ( X < 20 )$

(ii) $\text{P} ( X \geq 29 )$

(iii) $\text{P} ( 20 \leq X < 29 )$
parts.solutionMd:
(i)

Standardise using the formula

$Z = \frac{X-μ}{σ}$

Substitute $μ = 23$ and $σ = 4$

`\text{P}(X < 20) = \text{P}\left(Z < \dfrac{20 - 23}{4}\right) = \text{P}(Z < -0.75)`

The $z$-value is negative, so use symmetry: the area to the left of −0.75 equals the area to the right of 0.75

![Two standard normal curves side by side: the first has the area to the left of −0.75 shaded, the second has the equal area to the right of 0.75 shaded](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-probability-and-statistics-1/statistical-distributions/normal-distribution/assets/031-two-standard-normal-curves-side-by-side-the-firs.png)

$\text{P} ( X < 20 ) = 1 - Φ ( 0 . 75 )$

**[M1]**

In the table of the normal distribution function in the formula booklet, the 0.7 row and the 5 column give

$Φ ( 0 . 75 ) = 0 . 7734$

$\text{P} ( X < 20 ) = 1 - 0 . 7734 = 0 . 2266$

**Final answer:** $\text{P} ( X < 20 ) = 0 . 227$** (3 s.f.)**

**[A1]**

(ii)

![Normal curve with the mean 23 marked by a dashed line and the area to the right of 29 shaded](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-probability-and-statistics-1/statistical-distributions/normal-distribution/assets/032-normal-curve-with-the-mean-23-marked-by-a-dashed.png)

Standardise 29 in the same way

`\text{P}(X \geq 29) = \text{P}\left(Z \geq \dfrac{29 - 23}{4}\right) = \text{P}(Z \geq 1.5)`

The area to the right is 1 minus the area to the left

$\text{P} ( X \geq 29 ) = 1 - Φ ( 1 . 5 )$

**[M1]**

In the same table, the 1.5 row and the 0 column give

$Φ ( 1 . 5 ) = 0 . 9332$

$\text{P} ( X \geq 29 ) = 1 - 0 . 9332 = 0 . 0668$

**Final answer:** $\text{P} ( X \geq 29 ) = 0 . 0668$** (3 s.f.)**

**[A1]**

(iii)

The area between 20 and 29 is everything except the two tails found in (i) and (ii)

![Normal curve with the mean 23 marked by a dashed line and the area between 20 and 29 shaded](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-probability-and-statistics-1/statistical-distributions/normal-distribution/assets/033-normal-curve-with-the-mean-23-marked-by-a-dashed.png)

$\text{P} ( 20 \leq X < 29 ) = 1 - 0 . 2266 - 0 . 0668$

**[M1]**

$\text{P} ( 20 \leq X < 29 ) = 0 . 7066$

**Final answer:** $\text{P} ( 20 \leq X < 29 ) = 0 . 707$** (3 s.f.)**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Standardising 20 with 23 and 4, and 1 − Φ(0.75) (or Φ(−0.75)) found.
> 
> **A1**: 0.227, or answers which round to 0.227.
> 
> **M1**: Standardising 29 with 23 and 4, and 1 − Φ(1.5) found.
> 
> **A1**: 0.0668, or answers which round to 0.0668.
> 
> **M1**: 1 − (their (i)) − (their (ii)), or Φ(1.5) − Φ(−0.75), or an equivalent method giving a probability.
> 
> **A1**: 0.707, or answers which round to 0.707.
> 
> Dividing by 16 instead of 4 does not score the method marks. If 0.227, 0.0668 or 0.707 is given with no working, for example straight from a calculator, award 1 mark only for that answer.

parts.problemMd:
The random variable `Y \sim \text{N}(100, \; 225)`.

Find

(i) $\text{P} ( Y \leq 90 )$

(ii) $\text{P} ( Y > 140 )$

(iii) $\text{P} ( 85 \leq Y \leq 115 )$
parts.solutionMd:
(i)

To find the standard deviation, square root the variance

$σ = \sqrt{225} = 15$

Standardise using the formula

$Z = \frac{X-μ}{σ}$

Substitute $μ = 100$ and $σ = 15$

`\text{P}(Y \leq 90) = \text{P}\left(Z \leq \dfrac{90 - 100}{15}\right) = \text{P}(Z \leq -0.667)`

The $z$-value is negative, so use symmetry: the area to the left of −0.667 equals the area to the right of 0.667

![Two standard normal curves side by side: the first has the area to the left of −0.667 shaded, the second has the equal area to the right of 0.667 shaded](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-probability-and-statistics-1/statistical-distributions/normal-distribution/assets/034-two-standard-normal-curves-side-by-side-the-firs.png)

$\text{P} ( Y \leq 90 ) = 1 - Φ ( 0 . 667 )$

**[M1]**

To find $Φ ( 0 . 667 )$, use the table of the normal distribution function in the formula booklet. The 0.6 row and the 6 column give

$Φ ( 0 . 66 ) = 0 . 7454$

For the third decimal place, 7, look in the ADD columns: ADD 7 in the 0.6 row is 23, so add 0.0023

$Φ ( 0 . 667 ) = 0 . 7454 + 0 . 0023 = 0 . 7477$

$\text{P} ( Y \leq 90 ) = 1 - 0 . 7477 = 0 . 2523$

**Final answer:** $\text{P} ( Y \leq 90 ) = 0 . 252$** (3 s.f.)**

**[A1]**

(ii)

![Normal curve with the mean 100 marked by a dashed line and the very small area to the right of 140 shaded, with an arrow labelled P(Y > 140) pointing to it](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-probability-and-statistics-1/statistical-distributions/normal-distribution/assets/035-normal-curve-with-the-mean-100-marked-by-a-dashe.png)

Standardise 140 in the same way

`\text{P}(Y > 140) = \text{P}\left(Z > \dfrac{140 - 100}{15}\right) = \text{P}(Z > 2.667)`

The area to the right is 1 minus the area to the left

$\text{P} ( Y > 140 ) = 1 - Φ ( 2 . 667 )$

**[M1]**

In the same table, the 2.6 row and the 6 column give

$Φ ( 2 . 66 ) = 0 . 9961$

ADD 7 in the 2.6 row is 1, so add 0.0001

$Φ ( 2 . 667 ) = 0 . 9961 + 0 . 0001 = 0 . 9962$

$\text{P} ( Y > 140 ) = 1 - 0 . 9962$

$\text{P} ( Y > 140 ) = 0 . 0038$

**[A1]**

(iii)

85 and 115 are each one standard deviation from the mean, so the interval is symmetrical

![Normal curve with the mean 100 marked by a dashed line and the area between 85 and 115 shaded](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-probability-and-statistics-1/statistical-distributions/normal-distribution/assets/036-normal-curve-with-the-mean-100-marked-by-a-dashe.png)

$\text{P} ( 85 \leq Y \leq 115 ) = \text{P} ( - 1 \leq Z \leq 1 )$

The area between −1 and 1 is the area to the left of 1 minus the area to the left of −1

$\text{P} ( - 1 \leq Z \leq 1 ) = Φ ( 1 ) - Φ ( - 1 )$

The table only gives positive values of $z$. By symmetry, the area to the left of −1 equals the area to the right of 1

$Φ ( - 1 ) = 1 - Φ ( 1 )$

Substitute this into the first line

`\text{P}(-1 \leq Z \leq 1) = \mathrm{\Phi}(1) - \left(1 - \mathrm{\Phi}(1)\right)`

$\text{P} ( - 1 \leq Z \leq 1 ) = 2 Φ ( 1 ) - 1$

**[M1]**

In the same table, the 1.0 row and the 0 column give

$Φ ( 1 ) = 0 . 8413$

$\text{P} ( 85 \leq Y \leq 115 ) = 2 \times 0 . 8413 - 1 = 0 . 6826$

**Final answer:** $\text{P} ( 85 \leq Y \leq 115 ) = 0 . 683$** (3 s.f.)**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Standardising 90 with 100 and 15, and 1 − Φ(0.667) (or Φ(−0.667)) found.
> 
> **A1**: 0.252, or answers which round to 0.252. Accept 0.2525.
> 
> **M1**: Standardising 140 with 100 and 15, and 1 − Φ(2.667) found.
> 
> **A1**: 0.0038, or 0.00383 from a calculator.
> 
> **M1**: Both of ±1 used as z-values and the area from Φ values of ± the same number, such as Φ(1) − (1 − Φ(1)) or 2Φ(1) − 1.
> 
> **A1**: 0.683, or answers which round to 0.683.
> 
> Dividing by 225 instead of 15 does not score the method marks. If 0.252, 0.0038 or 0.683 is given with no working, for example straight from a calculator, award 1 mark only for that answer.

parts.problemMd:
The times taken, in minutes, by employees at a large company to complete a particular task are normally distributed with mean 50 and standard deviation 7.

97.5% of employees take less than $a$ minutes to complete the task. Find the value of $a$.
parts.solutionMd:
Let $T$ be the time taken, in minutes, so `T \sim \text{N}(50, \; 7^{2})` and $\text{P} ( T < a ) = 0 . 975$

![Normal curve with the mean 50 marked by a dashed line and the area 0.975 to the left of a shaded](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-probability-and-statistics-1/statistical-distributions/normal-distribution/assets/037-normal-curve-with-the-mean-50-marked-by-a-dashed.png)

0.975 is in the table of critical values for the normal distribution in the formula booklet

$\text{P} ( Z < z ) = 0 . 975 \Rightarrow z = 1 . 960$

**[B1]**

Standardise using the formula

$Z = \frac{X-μ}{σ}$

Substitute $X = a$, $μ = 50$ and $σ = 7$, and set the result equal to this $z$-value

$\frac{a-50}{7} = 1 . 960$

**[M1]**

$a = 50 + 1 . 960 \times 7 = 63 . 72$

**Final answer:** $a = 63 . 7$** (3 s.f.)**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: z = 1.960, or −1.960 used consistently. Accept 1.96.
> 
> **M1**: (a − 50)/7 equated to their z-value. Equating to 0.975 or 0.025, or dividing by 49, does not score.
> 
> **A1**: a = 63.7, or answers which round to 63.7.

parts.problemMd: Only 0.1% of employees take more than $b$ minutes to complete the task. Find the value of $b$.
parts.solutionMd:
$\text{P} ( T > b ) = 0 . 001$, so the area to the left of $b$ is 0.999

![Normal curve with the mean 50 marked by a dashed line and the small area 0.001 to the right of b shaded](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-probability-and-statistics-1/statistical-distributions/normal-distribution/assets/038-normal-curve-with-the-mean-50-marked-by-a-dashed.png)

0.999 is in the table of critical values for the normal distribution in the formula booklet

$\text{P} ( Z < z ) = 0 . 999 \Rightarrow z = 3 . 090$

**[B1]**

Standardise using the formula

$Z = \frac{X-μ}{σ}$

Substitute $X = b$, $μ = 50$ and $σ = 7$, and set the result equal to this $z$-value

$\frac{b-50}{7} = 3 . 090$

**[M1]**

$b = 50 + 3 . 090 \times 7 = 71 . 63$

**Final answer:** $b = 71 . 6$** (3 s.f.)**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: z = 3.090, or −3.090 used consistently. Accept 3.09.
> 
> **M1**: (b − 50)/7 equated to their z-value. Equating to 0.001 or 0.999, or dividing by 49, does not score.
> 
> **A1**: b = 71.6, or answers which round to 71.6.

parts.problemMd:
The lengths of the leaves of a certain type of tree are normally distributed with mean $μ$ cm and standard deviation 6 cm. The probability that a randomly chosen leaf has a length less than 51 cm is 0.8665.

Find the value of $μ$.
parts.solutionMd:
Let $L$ be the length, in cm, so `L \sim \text{N}(\mu, \; 6^{2})` and $\text{P} ( L < 51 ) = 0 . 8665$

![Normal curve with the mean μ marked by a dashed line and the area 0.8665 to the left of 51 shaded](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-probability-and-statistics-1/statistical-distributions/normal-distribution/assets/043-normal-curve-with-the-mean-marked-by-a-dashed-li.png)

0.8665 is in the body of the table of the normal distribution function in the formula booklet, in the 1.1 row and the 1 column

$Φ ( z ) = 0 . 8665 \Rightarrow z = 1 . 11$

**[B1]**

0.8665 is more than 0.5, so 51 is above the mean and its $z$-value is positive. Standardise using the formula

$Z = \frac{X-μ}{σ}$

Substitute $X = 51$ and $σ = 6$, and set the result equal to this $z$-value

$\frac{51-μ}{6} = 1 . 11$

**[M1]**

$51 - μ = 6 . 66$

$μ = 44 . 34$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: z = 1.11, or −1.11 used consistently.
> 
> **M1**: (51 − μ)/6 equated to their z-value. Equating to 0.8665 or 0.1335, or dividing by 36, does not score.
> 
> **A1**: μ = 44.34, or answers which round to 44.3.

parts.problemMd:
The masses of peaches grown in an orchard are normally distributed with mean 93 grams and standard deviation $σ$ grams. The probability that a randomly chosen peach has a mass greater than 101 grams is 0.0735.

Find the value of $σ$.
parts.solutionMd:
Let $M$ be the mass, in grams, so `M \sim \text{N}(93, \; \sigma^{2})` and $\text{P} ( M > 101 ) = 0 . 0735$

![Normal curve with the mean 93 marked by a dashed line and the area 0.0735 to the right of 101 shaded](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-probability-and-statistics-1/statistical-distributions/normal-distribution/assets/044-normal-curve-with-the-mean-93-marked-by-a-dashed.png)

The area to the left of 101 is

$Φ ( z ) = 1 - 0 . 0735 = 0 . 9265$

0.9265 is in the body of the table of the normal distribution function in the formula booklet, in the 1.4 row and the 5 column

$z = 1 . 45$

**[B1]**

Standardise using the formula

$Z = \frac{X-μ}{σ}$

Substitute $X = 101$ and $μ = 93$, and set the result equal to this $z$-value

$\frac{101-93}{σ} = 1 . 45$

**[M1]**

$1 . 45 σ = 8$

$σ = \frac{8}{1.45} = 5 . 5172 \dots$

**Final answer:** $σ = 5 . 52$** (3 s.f.)**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: z = 1.45, or −1.45 used consistently.
> 
> **M1**: (101 − 93)/σ equated to their z-value. Equating to 0.0735 or 0.9265 does not score.
> 
> **A1**: σ = 5.52, or answers which round to 5.52.

parts.problemMd:
The times, in minutes, that customers spend waiting at a bank are normally distributed with mean 10 and standard deviation 3.

(i) Given that 40% of customers wait for less than $a$ minutes, find the value of $a$ correct to 2 decimal places.

(ii) Given that 25% of customers wait for more than $b$ minutes, find the value of $b$ correct to 2 decimal places.
parts.solutionMd:
(i)

Let $T$ be the waiting time, in minutes, so `T \sim \text{N}(10, \; 3^{2})` and $\text{P} ( T < a ) = 0 . 4$

![Normal curve with the mean 10 marked by a dashed line, the area 0.4 to the left of a shaded, and the area 0.25 to the right of b shaded](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-probability-and-statistics-1/statistical-distributions/normal-distribution/assets/048-normal-curve-with-the-mean-10-marked-by-a-dashed.png)

0.4 is less than 0.5, so $a$ is below the mean and its $z$-value is negative. By symmetry, the area to the left of $- z$ is 0.6

$Φ ( - z ) = 0 . 6$

In the table of the normal distribution function in the formula booklet, the nearest value below 0.6 is in the 0.2 row and the 5 column, $Φ ( 0 . 25 ) = 0 . 5987$

$0 . 6 - 0 . 5987 = 0 . 0013$

In the 0.2 row, 13 lies between ADD 3 (12) and ADD 4 (15), so take the third decimal place halfway

$- z = 0 . 2535 \Rightarrow z = - 0 . 2535$

**[B1]**

Standardise using the formula

$Z = \frac{X-μ}{σ}$

Substitute $X = a$, $μ = 10$ and $σ = 3$, and set the result equal to this $z$-value

$\frac{a-10}{3} = - 0 . 2535$

**[M1]**

$a = 10 - 0 . 2535 \times 3 = 9 . 2395$

**Final answer:** $a = 9 . 24$** (2 d.p.)**

**[A1]**

(ii)

$\text{P} ( T > b ) = 0 . 25$, so the area to the left of $b$ is 0.75, which is in the table of critical values for the normal distribution in the formula booklet

$Φ ( z ) = 0 . 75 \Rightarrow z = 0 . 674$

**[B1]**

Standardise $b$ in the same way and set the result equal to this $z$-value

$\frac{b-10}{3} = 0 . 674$

**[M1]**

$b = 10 + 0 . 674 \times 3 = 12 . 022$

**Final answer:** $b = 12 . 02$** (2 d.p.)**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: z = −0.253 for (i), accepting any value from −0.2535 to −0.253 (or the positive value used consistently).
> 
> **M1**: (a − 10)/3 equated to their z-value. Equating to 0.4 or 0.6, or dividing by 9, does not score.
> 
> **A1**: a = 9.24.
> 
> **B1**: z = 0.674 for (ii).
> 
> **M1**: (b − 10)/3 equated to their z-value. Equating to 0.25 or 0.75 does not score.
> 
> **A1**: b = 12.02.

parts.problemMd: Find the probability that a randomly chosen customer waits for between $a$ minutes and $b$ minutes.
parts.solutionMd:
The whole area under the curve is 1. The area to the left of $a$ is 0.4 and the area to the right of $b$ is 0.25, so the area between them is what remains

![Normal curve with the mean 10 marked, the area 0.4 to the left of a and the area 0.25 to the right of b labelled, and the area between a and b shaded](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-probability-and-statistics-1/statistical-distributions/normal-distribution/assets/049-normal-curve-with-the-mean-10-marked-the-area-0-.png)

$\text{P} ( a < T < b ) = 1 - 0 . 4 - 0 . 25$

**[M1]**

$\text{P} ( a < T < b ) = 0 . 35$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: 1 − 0.4 − 0.25, or an equivalent such as 0.75 − 0.4, or the area from their Φ values.
> 
> **A1**: 0.35. Accept answers which round to 0.35 from recalculating with the values of a and b.

parts.problemMd:
The lengths of a particular species of fish are normally distributed. 2.5% of these fish are longer than 36.88 cm and 10% are shorter than 27.16 cm.

Find the mean and the standard deviation of the lengths of these fish.
parts.solutionMd:
Let $L$ be the length, in cm, so `L \sim \text{N}(\mu, \; \sigma^{2})`, with $\text{P} ( L > 36 . 88 ) = 0 . 025$ and $\text{P} ( L < 27 . 16 ) = 0 . 1$

![Normal curve with the mean μ marked by a dashed line, the area 0.1 to the left of 27.16 shaded, and the area 0.025 to the right of 36.88 shaded](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-probability-and-statistics-1/statistical-distributions/normal-distribution/assets/030-normal-curve-with-the-mean-marked-by-a-dashed-li.png)

The area to the left of 36.88 is 0.975, which is in the table of critical values for the normal distribution in the formula booklet

$z_{1} = 1 . 960$

**[B1]**

27.16 is below the mean with 0.1 to its left, so its $z$-value is the negative of the critical value for 0.9

$z_{2} = - 1 . 282$

**[B1]**

Standardise using the formula

$Z = \frac{X-μ}{σ}$

Substitute each length and set the result equal to its $z$-value

$\frac{36.88-μ}{σ} = 1 . 960$

**[M1]**

$\frac{27.16-μ}{σ} = - 1 . 282$

Rearrange each into a linear equation

$μ + 1 . 960 σ = 36 . 88$

$μ - 1 . 282 σ = 27 . 16$

Subtract the second equation from the first to eliminate $μ$

$3 . 242 σ = 9 . 72$

$σ = \frac{9.72}{3.242} = 2 . 99815 \dots$

**[M1]**

Substitute the unrounded $σ$ into the first equation

$μ = 36 . 88 - 1 . 960 \times 2 . 99815 \dots = 31 . 0036 \dots$

**Final answer:** $μ = 31 . 0 ,  σ = 3 . 00$** (3 s.f.)**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: z = ±1.960 seen (accept 1.96).
> 
> **B1**: z = ±1.282 seen.
> 
> **M1**: One standardisation of 36.88 or 27.16 with μ and σ, equated to a z-value. Equating to a probability (0.025, 0.975, 0.1 or 0.9), or using σ², does not score.
>
