> 
> **A1**: $p - 4 q = \frac{2}{15}$ reached from that equation with no errors, since the result is given.

parts.problemMd: Write down a second equation involving $p$ and $q$.
parts.solutionMd:
The probabilities sum to 1

$p + \frac{1}{2} + q + \frac{1}{15} + q = 1$

$p + 2 q = \frac{13}{30}$

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: A correct equation from the probabilities summing to 1, simplified or unsimplified.

parts.problemMd: Hence find the values of $p$ and $q$.
parts.solutionMd:
The equation from part (a) is

$p - 4 q = \frac{2}{15}$

The equation from part (b) is

$p + 2 q = \frac{13}{30}$

Subtract the equation from part (a) from the equation from part (b) to eliminate $p$

$( p + 2 q ) - ( p - 4 q ) = \frac{13}{30} - \frac{2}{15}$

$6 q = \frac{3}{10}$

**[M1]**

$q = \frac{1}{20}$

Substitute into $p + 2 q = \frac{13}{30}$

$p = \frac{13}{30} - \frac{2}{20} = \frac{13}{30} - \frac{3}{30}$

$p = \frac{1}{3} ,  q = \frac{1}{20}$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Solving the two equations by substitution or elimination to find one of the unknowns.
> 
> **A1**: $p = \frac{1}{3}$ and $q = \frac{1}{20}$.

parts.problemMd: Find $\text{Var} ( X )$.
parts.solutionMd:
| $x$ | −2 | 0 | 2 | 4 | 6 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $\text{P} ( X = x )$ | $\frac{1}{3}$ | $\frac{1}{2}$ | $\frac{1}{20}$ | $\frac{1}{15}$ | $\frac{1}{20}$ |

Use `\text{Var}(X) = \sum x^{2}p - \left[\text{E}(X)\right]^{2}` with $\text{E} ( X ) = 0$

`\text{Var}(X) = \left(-2\right)^{2} \times \dfrac{1}{3} + 0^{2} \times \dfrac{1}{2} + 2^{2} \times \dfrac{1}{20} + 4^{2} \times \dfrac{1}{15} + 6^{2} \times \dfrac{1}{20} - 0^{2}`

**[M1]**

$\text{Var} ( X ) = \frac{4}{3} + \frac{1}{5} + \frac{16}{15} + \frac{9}{5}$

$\text{Var} ( X ) = \frac{22}{5}$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: $\sum x^{2} p$ with the values of $p$ and $q$ found, minus the square of the mean. Accept unsimplified.
> 
> **A1**: $\frac{22}{5}$ or 4.4.

parts.problemMd:
Leonardo has a biased spinner with six sectors labelled 0, 1, 1, 2, 3 and 5. The probability of the spinner landing on each sector is shown in the following table.

| Number on sector | 0 | 1 | 1 | 2 | 3 | 5 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Probability | $\frac{6}{20}$ | $p$ | $\frac{3}{20}$ | $\frac{5}{20}$ | $\frac{3}{20}$ | $\frac{1}{20}$ |

Find the value of $p$.
parts.solutionMd:
The six probabilities sum to 1

$\frac{6}{20} + p + \frac{3}{20} + \frac{5}{20} + \frac{3}{20} + \frac{1}{20} = 1$

$p + \frac{18}{20} = 1$

$p = \frac{2}{20}$

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: $p = \frac{2}{20}$, or equivalent such as $\frac{1}{10}$ or 0.1.

parts.problemMd:
Leonardo spins the spinner once. The random variable $X$ denotes the number on the sector where the spinner lands.

Find the probability that

(i) $X$ is no more than 1,

(ii) $X$ is at least 3.
parts.solutionMd:
| Number on sector | 0 | 1 | 1 | 2 | 3 | 5 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Probability | $\frac{6}{20}$ | $\frac{2}{20}$ | $\frac{3}{20}$ | $\frac{5}{20}$ | $\frac{3}{20}$ | $\frac{1}{20}$ |

(i)

"No more than 1" means $X = 0$ or $X = 1$, and a score of 1 comes from either sector labelled 1

$\text{P} ( X \leq 1 ) = \frac{6}{20} + \frac{2}{20} + \frac{3}{20}$

$\text{P} ( X \leq 1 ) = \frac{11}{20}$

**[B1]**

(ii)

"At least 3" means $X = 3$ or $X = 5$

$\text{P} ( X \geq 3 ) = \frac{3}{20} + \frac{1}{20}$

$\text{P} ( X \geq 3 ) = \frac{1}{5}$

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: $\frac{11}{20}$ or 0.55.
> 
> **B1**: $\frac{1}{5}$, $\frac{4}{20}$ or 0.2.

parts.problemMd: Find the mean and the standard deviation of $X$.
parts.solutionMd:
Combine the two sectors labelled 1

$\text{P} ( X = 1 ) = \frac{2}{20} + \frac{3}{20} = \frac{5}{20}$

| Number on sector | 0 | 1 | 2 | 3 | 5 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Probability | $\frac{6}{20}$ | $\frac{5}{20}$ | $\frac{5}{20}$ | $\frac{3}{20}$ | $\frac{1}{20}$ |

The mean of $X$ is its expected value, so use $\text{E} ( X ) = \sum x p$

$\text{E} ( X ) = 0 \times \frac{6}{20} + 1 \times \frac{5}{20} + 2 \times \frac{5}{20} + 3 \times \frac{3}{20} + 5 \times \frac{1}{20}$

**[M1]**

$\text{E} ( X ) = \frac{29}{20} = 1 . 45$

**[A1]**

Use `\text{Var}(X) = \sum x^{2}p - \left[\text{E}(X)\right]^{2}`

$\text{Var} ( X ) = 0^{2} \times \frac{6}{20} + 1^{2} \times \frac{5}{20} + 2^{2} \times \frac{5}{20} + 3^{2} \times \frac{3}{20} + 5^{2} \times \frac{1}{20} - 1 . 45^{2}$

**[M1]**

$\text{Var} ( X ) = \frac{77}{20} - 2 . 1025 = 1 . 7475$

The standard deviation is the square root of the variance

$\sqrt{1.7475} = 1 . 32193 \dots$

**Final answer:** $\text{Standard deviation} = 1 . 32$** (3 s.f.)**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: $\sum x p$ with all terms, using the value of $p$ found. Accept unsimplified.
> 
> **A1**: Mean of $\frac{29}{20}$ or 1.45.
> 
> **M1**: $\sum x^{2} p$ minus the square of the mean. Accept unsimplified.
> 
> **A1**: Standard deviation which rounds to 1.32. The exact form $\frac{\sqrt{699}}{20}$ is also accepted.

parts.problemMd:
Leonardo spins the spinner twice and adds the two scores together.

Find the probability that his total score is 5.
parts.solutionMd:
| Number on sector | 0 | 1 | 2 | 3 | 5 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Probability | $\frac{6}{20}$ | $\frac{5}{20}$ | $\frac{5}{20}$ | $\frac{3}{20}$ | $\frac{1}{20}$ |

A total of 5 comes from four ordered scenarios: (0, 5), (5, 0), (2, 3) and (3, 2)

$\text{P} ( 0 ,  5 ) = \text{P} ( 5 ,  0 ) = \frac{6}{20} \times \frac{1}{20} = \frac{6}{400}$

**[B1]**

$\text{P} ( 2 ,  3 ) = \text{P} ( 3 ,  2 ) = \frac{5}{20} \times \frac{3}{20} = \frac{15}{400}$

Add the four scenarios

$\text{P} ( \text{total} = 5 ) = \frac{6}{400} + \frac{6}{400} + \frac{15}{400} + \frac{15}{400} = \frac{42}{400}$

**[M1]**

$\text{P} ( \text{total} = 5 ) = \frac{21}{200}$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: One scenario probability correct, e.g. $\frac{6}{20} \times \frac{1}{20}$.
> 
> **M1**: The probabilities of all four scenarios added, with none repeated or missing.
> 
> **A1**: $\frac{21}{200}$ or 0.105.

parts.problemMd:
Three biased coins are tossed. For each coin, the probability of obtaining a head is $\frac{3}{5}$. The random variable $X$ is the number of heads obtained minus the number of tails obtained.

Draw up the probability distribution table for $X$.
parts.solutionMd:
For each coin, $\text{P} ( \text{head} ) = \frac{3}{5}$ and $\text{P} ( \text{tail} ) = \frac{2}{5}$. List the outcomes by the number of heads, and find $X$ for each

*3 heads, 0 tails (HHH): X = 3*

*2 heads, 1 tail (HHT, HTH, THH): X = 1*

*1 head, 2 tails (HTT, THT, TTH): X = −1*

*0 heads, 3 tails (TTT): X = −3*

Multiply the probabilities for each outcome, and count the arrangements

`\text{P}(X = 3) = \left(\dfrac{3}{5}\right)^{3} = \dfrac{27}{125}`

`\text{P}(X = 1) = 3 \times \left(\dfrac{3}{5}\right)^{2} \times \dfrac{2}{5} = \dfrac{54}{125}`

`\text{P}(X = -1) = 3 \times \dfrac{3}{5} \times \left(\dfrac{2}{5}\right)^{2} = \dfrac{36}{125}`

`\text{P}(X = -3) = \left(\dfrac{2}{5}\right)^{3} = \dfrac{8}{125}`

| $x$ | **Final answer:** **−3** | **Final answer:** **−1** | **Final answer:** **1** | **Final answer:** **3** |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| $\text{P} ( X = x )$ | $\frac{8}{125}$ | $\frac{36}{125}$ | $\frac{54}{125}$ | $\frac{27}{125}$ |

**[B1 B1 B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: Table with the values −3, −1, 1 and 3 only, and at least one correct probability.
> 
> **B1**: Two of the four probabilities correct.
> 
> **B1**: All four probabilities correct, or four probabilities which sum to 1 with at least two correct. Decimals correct to 3 significant figures (0.064, 0.288, 0.432, 0.216) are accepted.

parts.problemMd:
The random variable $X$ takes the values −1, 1, 3 and 5 only.

Show that $\text{P} ( X = x ) = \frac{x^{2}}{30}$ cannot be the probability distribution of $X$.
parts.solutionMd:
For a probability distribution, the probabilities must sum to 1. Add the four probabilities

`\dfrac{\left(-1\right)^{2}}{30} + \dfrac{1^{2}}{30} + \dfrac{3^{2}}{30} + \dfrac{5^{2}}{30} = \dfrac{1 + 1 + 9 + 25}{30}`

**[M1]**

$= \frac{36}{30} = \frac{6}{5}$

**Final answer:** **The probabilities sum to 6/5, not 1, so this cannot be the probability distribution of X**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: The four probabilities added, with each value of $x$ substituted.
> 
> **A1**: A total of $\frac{36}{30}$ or $\frac{6}{5}$ (or 1.2), with the conclusion that the probabilities do not sum to 1.

parts.problemMd:
It is given instead that $\text{P} ( X = x ) = \frac{x^{2}}{k}$, where $k$ is a constant.

Find the value of $k$.
parts.solutionMd:
The probabilities sum to 1

`\dfrac{\left(-1\right)^{2}}{k} + \dfrac{1^{2}}{k} + \dfrac{3^{2}}{k} + \dfrac{5^{2}}{k} = 1`

**[M1]**

$\frac{36}{k} = 1$

$k = 36$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Sum of the four probabilities in terms of $k$ set equal to 1.
> 
> **A1**: $k = 36$.

parts.problemMd: Find $\text{P} ( X > 0 )$.
parts.solutionMd:
Every value except $- 1$ is positive, so subtract $\text{P} ( X = - 1 )$ from 1

`\text{P}(X > 0) = 1 - \text{P}(X = -1) = 1 - \dfrac{\left(-1\right)^{2}}{36}`

**[M1]**

$\text{P} ( X > 0 ) = \frac{35}{36}$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: $1 - \text{P} ( X = - 1 )$, or $\text{P} ( X = 1 ) + \text{P} ( X = 3 ) + \text{P} ( X = 5 )$, using the value of $k$ found.
> 
> **A1**: $\frac{35}{36}$, or answers which round to 0.972.

parts.problemMd:
The random variable $X$ takes the values 0, 1, 3, 6, 10 and 15 only. It is given that

$\text{P} ( X = 0 ) = \text{P} ( X = 1 ) = 0 . 21$

$\text{P} ( X = 10 ) = \text{P} ( X = 15 ) = 0 . 11$

$\text{P} ( X = x ) = k x$ for $x = 3$ and $x = 6$

where $k$ is a constant.

Find the value of $k$.
parts.solutionMd:
Write $\text{P} ( X = 3 ) = 3 k$ and $\text{P} ( X = 6 ) = 6 k$, then set the sum of the six probabilities equal to 1

$0 . 21 + 0 . 21 + 3 k + 6 k + 0 . 11 + 0 . 11 = 1$

**[M1]**

$9 k + 0 . 64 = 1$

$k = 0 . 04$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: All six probabilities, with $3 k$ and $6 k$, added and set equal to 1. Accept unsimplified.
> 
> **A1**: $k = 0 . 04$.

parts.problemMd: Draw up the probability distribution table for $X$.
parts.solutionMd:
Substitute $k = 0 . 04$ for $x = 3$ and $x = 6$

$\text{P} ( X = 3 ) = 3 \times 0 . 04 = 0 . 12$

$\text{P} ( X = 6 ) = 6 \times 0 . 04 = 0 . 24$

| $x$ | **Final answer:** **0** | **Final answer:** **1** | **Final answer:** **3** | **Final answer:** **6** | **Final answer:** **10** | **Final answer:** **15** |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $\text{P} ( X = x )$ | **Final answer:** **0.21** | **Final answer:** **0.21** | **Final answer:** **0.12** | **Final answer:** **0.24** | **Final answer:** **0.11** | **Final answer:** **0.11** |

**[B1 B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: Table with all six values of $x$ and at least one correct probability.

parts.problemMd: Find $\text{P} ( 3 < X \leq 14 )$.

The discrete random variable $X$ has the probability distribution shown in the following table.

| $x$ | −2 | 0 | 2 | 4 | 6 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $\text{P} ( X = x )$ | $p$ | $\frac{2}{15}$ | $\frac{1}{4}$ | $\frac{2}{15}$ | $p$ |

Without calculating the value of $p$, explain why $\text{E} ( X ) = 2$.
parts.solutionMd:
Look at how the values and their probabilities are arranged around 2

**Final answer:** **The values of x are symmetrical about 2 and so are their probabilities, so the distribution is symmetrical about 2 and E(X) = 2**

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: A statement that the distribution (both the values and their probabilities) is symmetrical about 2.

parts.problemMd: Find the value of $p$.
parts.solutionMd:
The probabilities sum to 1

$p + \frac{2}{15} + \frac{1}{4} + \frac{2}{15} + p = 1$

$2 p + \frac{31}{60} = 1$

$p = \frac{29}{120}$

**[B1]**

> **B1**: $p = \frac{29}{120}$, or answers which round to 0.242.

parts.problemMd: Find $\text{Var} ( X )$.
Find `\text{P}\left(X > \text{E}(X)\right)`.

The discrete random variable $X$ has the probability distribution shown in the following table.

| $x$ | 0 | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $\text{P} ( X = x )$ | $p$ | $p$ | 0.2 | 0.1 | $q$ |

Given that $\text{E} ( X ) = 2 . 45$, find the value of $p$ and the value of $q$.
parts.solutionMd:
The probabilities sum to 1

$p + p + 0 . 2 + 0 . 1 + q = 1$

$2 p + q = 0 . 7$

**[B1]**

Use $\text{E} ( X ) = \sum x p$ and set it equal to 2.45

$0 \times p + 1 \times p + 2 \times 0 . 2 + 3 \times 0 . 1 + 4 q = 2 . 45$

$p + 4 q = 1 . 75$

**[B1]**

Multiply the first equation by 4 and subtract the second to eliminate $q$

$8 p + 4 q - ( p + 4 q ) = 2 . 8 - 1 . 75$

$7 p = 1 . 05$

**[M1]**

$p = 0 . 15$

Substitute into $2 p + q = 0 . 7$

$q = 0 . 7 - 2 \times 0 . 15$

$p = 0 . 15 ,  q = 0 . 4$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: A correct equation from the probabilities summing to 1, simplified or unsimplified.
> 
> **B1**: A correct equation from $\text{E} ( X ) = 2 . 45$, simplified or unsimplified.
> 
> **M1**: Solving the two equations by substitution or elimination to find one of the unknowns.
> 
> **A1**: $p = 0 . 15$ and $q = 0 . 4$.

parts.problemMd: Find $\text{Var} ( X )$.
Find `\text{P}\left(X < \text{E}(X)\right)`.

The random variable $X$ has the probability distribution shown in the following table.

| $x$ | −1 | 1 | 2 |
|---|---|---|---|
| $\text{P} ( X = x )$ | $\frac{5}{12}$ | $p$ | $\frac{1}{4}$ |

Find the value of $p$.
parts.solutionMd:
The probabilities sum to 1

$\frac{5}{12} + p + \frac{1}{4} = 1$

$p = \frac{1}{3}$

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: $p = \frac{1}{3}$.

parts.problemMd:
Two independent observations of $X$ are taken. The random variable $Y$ is the sum of the two observations.

Complete the following probability distribution table for $Y$.

| $y$ | −2 | 0 | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $\text{P} ( Y = y )$ |   |   |   |   |   |   |
parts.solutionMd:
| $x$ | −1 | 1 | 2 |
|---|---|---|---|
| $\text{P} ( X = x )$ | $\frac{5}{12}$ | $\frac{1}{3}$ | $\frac{1}{4}$ |

A total of −2, 2 or 4 needs the same value twice, so square that probability

`\text{P}(Y = -2) = \left(\dfrac{5}{12}\right)^{2} = \dfrac{25}{144}`

`\text{P}(Y = 2) = \left(\dfrac{1}{3}\right)^{2} = \dfrac{16}{144}`

`\text{P}(Y = 4) = \left(\dfrac{1}{4}\right)^{2} = \dfrac{9}{144}`

A total of 0, 1 or 3 needs two different values, which can come in either order, so double the product

$\text{P} ( Y = 0 ) = 2 \times \frac{5}{12} \times \frac{1}{3} = \frac{40}{144}$

$\text{P} ( Y = 1 ) = 2 \times \frac{5}{12} \times \frac{1}{4} = \frac{30}{144}$

$\text{P} ( Y = 3 ) = 2 \times \frac{1}{3} \times \frac{1}{4} = \frac{24}{144}$

| $y$ | −2 | 0 | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $\text{P} ( Y = y )$ | $\frac{25}{144}$ | $\frac{40}{144}$ | $\frac{30}{144}$ | $\frac{16}{144}$ | $\frac{24}{144}$ | $\frac{9}{144}$ |

**[B1 B1 B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: At least one probability correct and linked to its value of $y$.
> 
> **B1**: At least three further probabilities correct. A total from two different values, such as $\text{P} ( Y = 0 )$, needs both orders ($2 \times$ the product).
> 
> **B1**: All six probabilities correct. Simplified fractions (such as $\frac{5}{18}$, $\frac{5}{24}$, $\frac{1}{9}$, $\frac{1}{6}$, $\frac{1}{16}$) and decimals correct to 3 significant figures are accepted.

Subtract $\text{P} ( Y = 0 )$ from 1

$\text{P} ( Y \neq 0 ) = \frac{13}{18}$

**[B1]**

(ii)

$Y < 0$ or $Y \geq 2$ means $Y = - 2 ,  2 ,  3 \text{or} 4$

$\text{P} ( Y < 0 \text{or} Y \geq 2 ) = \frac{37}{72}$

parts.problemMd:
Leonidas plays a game with a fair six-sided dice. He rolls the dice until either a 6 is obtained or he has rolled the dice four times. The random variable $X$ denotes the number of times the dice is rolled.

Draw up the probability distribution table for $X$.
parts.solutionMd:
The game stops at the first 6, so each earlier roll must be "not 6", with probability $\frac{5}{6}$

$\text{P} ( X = 1 ) = \frac{1}{6} = \frac{36}{216}$

$\text{P} ( X = 2 ) = \frac{5}{6} \times \frac{1}{6} = \frac{5}{36} = \frac{30}{216}$

`\text{P}(X = 3) = \left(\dfrac{5}{6}\right)^{2} \times \dfrac{1}{6} = \dfrac{25}{216}`

The game always stops after the fourth roll, so $X = 4$ only needs the first three rolls to be "not 6"

`\text{P}(X = 4) = \left(\dfrac{5}{6}\right)^{3} = \dfrac{125}{216}`

| $x$ | **Final answer:** **1** | **Final answer:** **2** | **Final answer:** **3** | **Final answer:** **4** |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| $\text{P} ( X = x )$ | $\frac{1}{6}$ | $\frac{5}{36}$ | $\frac{25}{216}$ | $\frac{125}{216}$ |

**[B1 B1 B1 B1]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The fourth roll ends the game whether or not it is a 6, so there is no final $\frac{1}{6}$ in $\text{P} ( X = 4 )$. A quick check is that your four probabilities sum to 1; with an extra factor of $\frac{1}{6}$ they would not.

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: Table with the values 1, 2, 3 and 4 only, and at least one correct probability.
> 
> **B1**: $\text{P} ( X = 2 ) = \frac{5}{36}$ correct.
> 
> **B1**: $\text{P} ( X = 3 ) = \frac{25}{216}$ correct.
> 
> **B1**: $\text{P} ( X = 4 ) = \frac{125}{216}$ correct, or four probabilities which sum to 1. Decimals correct to 3 significant figures are accepted throughout.

parts.problemMd:
Find the probability that the dice is rolled

(i) at most 3 times,

(ii) at least 3 times.
parts.solutionMd:
| $x$ | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| $\text{P} ( X = x )$ | $\frac{1}{6}$ | $\frac{5}{36}$ | $\frac{25}{216}$ | $\frac{125}{216}$ |

(i)

"At most 3 times" is every outcome except $X = 4$

$\text{P} ( X \leq 3 ) = 1 - \text{P} ( X = 4 ) = 1 - \frac{125}{216}$

$\text{P} ( X \leq 3 ) = \frac{91}{216}$

**[B1]**

(ii)

"At least 3 times" means $X = 3$ or $X = 4$

$\text{P} ( X \geq 3 ) = \frac{25}{216} + \frac{125}{216} = \frac{150}{216}$

$\text{P} ( X \geq 3 ) = \frac{25}{36}$

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: $\frac{91}{216}$, or answers which round to 0.421.
> 
> **B1**: $\frac{25}{36}$, or equivalent such as $\frac{150}{216}$, or answers which round to 0.694.

parts.problemMd: Find the mean and the standard deviation of $X$.
parts.solutionMd:
| $x$ | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| $\text{P} ( X = x )$ | $\frac{1}{6}$ | $\frac{5}{36}$ | $\frac{25}{216}$ | $\frac{125}{216}$ |

The mean of $X$ is its expected value, so use $\text{E} ( X ) = \sum x p$, with every probability over 216

$\text{E} ( X ) = 1 \times \frac{36}{216} + 2 \times \frac{30}{216} + 3 \times \frac{25}{216} + 4 \times \frac{125}{216}$

**[M1]**

**Final answer:** $\text{E} ( X ) = \frac{671}{216} = 3 . 11$** (3 s.f.)**

**[A1]**

Use `\text{Var}(X) = \sum x^{2}p - \left[\text{E}(X)\right]^{2}`

`\text{Var}(X) = 1^{2} \times \dfrac{36}{216} + 2^{2} \times \dfrac{30}{216} + 3^{2} \times \dfrac{25}{216} + 4^{2} \times \dfrac{125}{216} - \left(\dfrac{671}{216}\right)^{2}`

**[M1]**

`\text{Var}(X) = \dfrac{2381}{216} - \left(\dfrac{671}{216}\right)^{2} = 1.37292\ldots`

The standard deviation is the square root of the variance

$\sqrt{1.37292\dots} = 1 . 17171 \dots$

**Final answer:** $\text{Standard deviation} = 1 . 17$** (3 s.f.)**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: $\sum x p$ with all four terms from the table. Accept unsimplified.
> 
> **A1**: Mean of $\frac{671}{216}$, or answers which round to 3.11.
> 
> **M1**: $\sum x^{2} p$ minus the square of the mean. Accept unsimplified.
> 
> **A1**: Standard deviation which rounds to 1.17.

parts.problemMd:
The random variables $X$ and $Y$ are independent.

$X$ takes the values 1, 2, 3, 5, 8 and 11 only, each with probability $p$.

$Y$ takes the values 1, 3 and 6 only, and $\text{P} ( Y = y ) = \frac{q}{y}$, where $q$ is a constant.

Find the value of $p$ and the value of $q$.
parts.solutionMd:
$X$ has six equally likely values, and the probabilities sum to 1

$6 p = 1$

$p = \frac{1}{6}$

**[B1]**

For $Y$, the probabilities also sum to 1

$\frac{q}{1} + \frac{q}{3} + \frac{q}{6} = 1$

**[M1]**

$\frac{3q}{2} = 1$

$q = \frac{2}{3}$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: $p = \frac{1}{6}$.
> 
> **M1**: Sum of the three probabilities for $Y$ in terms of $q$ set equal to 1.
> 
> **A1**: $q = \frac{2}{3}$.

parts.problemMd: Find $\text{P} ( X > Y )$.
parts.solutionMd:
Each value of $X$ has probability $\frac{1}{6}$. Substitute $q = \frac{2}{3}$ into $\frac{q}{y}$ to find the probabilities for $Y$

| $y$ | 1 | 3 | 6 |
|---|---|---|---|
| $\text{P} ( Y = y )$ | $\frac{2}{3}$ | $\frac{2}{9}$ | $\frac{1}{9}$ |

Split by the value of $Y$: for each one, count the values of $X$ that are bigger

$\text{P} ( Y = 1 \text{and} X > 1 ) = \frac{2}{3} \times \frac{5}{6} = \frac{30}{54}$

**[B1]**

$\text{P} ( Y = 3 \text{and} X > 3 ) = \frac{2}{9} \times \frac{3}{6} = \frac{6}{54}$

$\text{P} ( Y = 6 \text{and} X > 6 ) = \frac{1}{9} \times \frac{2}{6} = \frac{2}{54}$

Add the three scenarios

$\text{P} ( X > Y ) = \frac{30}{54} + \frac{6}{54} + \frac{2}{54} = \frac{38}{54}$

**[M1]**

$\text{P} ( X > Y ) = \frac{19}{27}$

**[A1]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Splitting by the variable with fewer values keeps the number of cases down. Here conditioning on $Y$ gives three cases; listing by $X$ gives six, and it is easy to miss that $X = 8$ and $X = 11$ beat every value of $Y$.

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: One correct scenario probability, e.g. $\frac{2}{3} \times \frac{5}{6}$, or a single pair such as $\frac{1}{6} \times \frac{2}{3}$ for $X = 2 ,  Y = 1$.
> 
> **M1**: All the scenarios with $X > Y$ added, with none repeated or missing. Listing by the value of $X$ is equally valid.
> 
> **A1**: $\frac{19}{27}$, or answers which round to 0.704.

parts.problemMd:
Two biased coins are tossed and a fair spinner with three sectors numbered 1, 2 and 3 is spun. For each coin, the probability of obtaining a head is $\frac{1}{3}$. The random variable $X$ is the number of heads obtained multiplied by the number on the spinner.

Draw up the probability distribution table for $X$.
parts.solutionMd:
First find the probabilities for the number of heads, using $\text{P} ( \text{head} ) = \frac{1}{3}$ and $\text{P} ( \text{tail} ) = \frac{2}{3}$

$\text{P} ( 0 \text{heads} ) = \frac{2}{3} \times \frac{2}{3} = \frac{4}{9}$

$\text{P} ( 1 \text{head} ) = 2 \times \frac{1}{3} \times \frac{2}{3} = \frac{4}{9}$

$\text{P} ( 2 \text{heads} ) = \frac{1}{3} \times \frac{1}{3} = \frac{1}{9}$

Multiply each number of heads by each spinner score (1, 2 or 3) to find the possible values of $X$

*0 heads: X = 0*

*1 head: X = 1, 2 or 3*

*2 heads: X = 2, 4 or 6*

$X = 0 ,  1 ,  2 ,  3 ,  4 \text{or} 6$

**[B1]**

With no heads, $X = 0$ whatever the spinner shows

$\text{P} ( X = 0 ) = \frac{4}{9} = \frac{12}{27}$

Each other value needs a number of heads and a spinner score, each spinner score having probability $\frac{1}{3}$. A total of 2 can happen in two ways

$\text{P} ( X = 2 ) = \text{P} ( 1 \text{head, spinner} 2 ) + \text{P} ( 2 \text{heads, spinner} 1 ) = \frac{4}{9} \times \frac{1}{3} + \frac{1}{9} \times \frac{1}{3} = \frac{5}{27}$

**[M1]**

$\text{P} ( X = 1 ) = \frac{4}{9} \times \frac{1}{3} = \frac{4}{27}$

$\text{P} ( X = 3 ) = \frac{4}{9} \times \frac{1}{3} = \frac{4}{27}$

$\text{P} ( X = 4 ) = \frac{1}{9} \times \frac{1}{3} = \frac{1}{27}$

$\text{P} ( X = 6 ) = \frac{1}{9} \times \frac{1}{3} = \frac{1}{27}$

| $x$ | **Final answer:** **0** | **Final answer:** **1** | **Final answer:** **2** | **Final answer:** **3** | **Final answer:** **4** | **Final answer:** **6** |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $\text{P} ( X = x )$ | $\frac{12}{27}$ | $\frac{4}{27}$ | $\frac{5}{27}$ | $\frac{4}{27}$ | $\frac{1}{27}$ | $\frac{1}{27}$ |

**[A1 A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: The values 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 and 6 only, in a table or listed.
> 
> **M1**: $\text{P} ( X = 2 )$ found by adding the two ways of scoring 2 (one head with a 2, or two heads with a 1).
> 
> **A1**: At least three of the six probabilities correct.
> 
> **A1**: All six probabilities correct. Decimals correct to 3 significant figures are accepted.

parts.problemMd:
The random variable $X$ takes the values −3, −1, 1 and 3 only.

Show that

$\text{P} ( X = x ) = \frac{1}{3x^{2}}$ for $x = - 3 ,  - 1$

$\text{P} ( X = x ) = \frac{1}{3x^{3}}$ for $x = 1 ,  3$

cannot be the probability distribution of $X$.
parts.solutionMd:
For a probability distribution, the probabilities must sum to 1. Find each probability

$\text{P} ( X = - 3 ) = \frac{1}{3\times9} = \frac{1}{27}$

$\text{P} ( X = - 1 ) = \frac{1}{3\times1} = \frac{1}{3}$

$\text{P} ( X = 1 ) = \frac{1}{3\times1} = \frac{1}{3}$

$\text{P} ( X = 3 ) = \frac{1}{3\times27} = \frac{1}{81}$

Add them

$\frac{1}{27} + \frac{1}{3} + \frac{1}{3} + \frac{1}{81} = \frac{3+27+27+1}{81} = \frac{58}{81}$

**[M1]**

**Final answer:** **The probabilities sum to 58/81, not 1, so this cannot be the probability distribution of X**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: The four probabilities found and added.
> 
> **A1**: A total of $\frac{58}{81}$ (or answers which round to 0.716), with the conclusion that the probabilities do not sum to 1.

parts.problemMd:
It is given instead that

$\text{P} ( X = x ) = \frac{k}{x^{2}}$ for $x = - 3 ,  - 1$

$\text{P} ( X = x ) = \frac{k}{x^{3}}$ for $x = 1 ,  3$

where $k$ is a constant.

Find the exact value of $k$.
parts.solutionMd:
The probabilities sum to 1

`\dfrac{k}{\left(-3\right)^{2}} + \dfrac{k}{\left(-1\right)^{2}} + \dfrac{k}{1^{3}} + \dfrac{k}{3^{3}} = 1`

**[M1]**

$\frac{k}{9} + k + k + \frac{k}{27} = \frac{58k}{27} = 1$

$k = \frac{27}{58}$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Sum of the four probabilities in terms of $k$ set equal to 1, with the correct power in each term.
> 
> **A1**: $k = \frac{27}{58}$ exactly.

parts.problemMd: Find $\text{P} ( X < 2 )$.
parts.solutionMd:
Only $X = 3$ fails $X < 2$, so subtract its probability from 1

$\text{P} ( X < 2 ) = 1 - \text{P} ( X = 3 ) = 1 - \frac{k}{27} = 1 - \frac{1}{58}$

**[M1]**

$\text{P} ( X < 2 ) = \frac{57}{58}$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: $1 - \text{P} ( X = 3 )$, or the sum of the other three probabilities, using the value of $k$ found.
> 
> **A1**: $\frac{57}{58}$, or answers which round to 0.983.

parts.problemMd:
Leofranc plays a game at a school fair. It costs 2 dollars to play. He chooses a "lucky number" from 1 to 6, then rolls a fair six-sided dice until either his lucky number appears or he has rolled the dice four times.

If his lucky number appears on the first roll, he receives 5 dollars. If it first appears on the second, third or fourth roll, he receives 3 dollars, 2 dollars or 1 dollar respectively. If it has not appeared by the fourth roll, he receives nothing.

The random variable $W$ is Leofranc's profit, in dollars, from one game (the amount he receives minus the cost of playing). A negative profit means that he loses money.

Draw up the probability distribution table for $W$.
parts.solutionMd:
Subtract the 2-dollar cost from each amount received (5, 3, 2, 1 or 0 dollars) to find the possible values of $W$

$W = 3 ,  1 ,  0 ,  - 1 \text{or} - 2$

**[B1]**

On each roll, $\text{P} ( \text{lucky number} ) = \frac{1}{6}$, and every earlier roll must not show it

$\text{P} ( W = 3 ) = \frac{1}{6}$

$\text{P} ( W = 1 ) = \frac{5}{6} \times \frac{1}{6} = \frac{5}{36}$

`\text{P}(W = 0) = \left(\dfrac{5}{6}\right)^{2} \times \dfrac{1}{6} = \dfrac{25}{216}`

**[M1]**

`\text{P}(W = -1) = \left(\dfrac{5}{6}\right)^{3} \times \dfrac{1}{6} = \dfrac{125}{1296}`

He receives nothing only if none of the four rolls shows his lucky number

`\text{P}(W = -2) = \left(\dfrac{5}{6}\right)^{4} = \dfrac{625}{1296}`

| $w$ | **Final answer:** **−2** | **Final answer:** **−1** | **Final answer:** **0** | **Final answer:** **1** | **Final answer:** **3** |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $\text{P} ( W = w )$ | $\frac{625}{1296}$ | $\frac{125}{1296}$ | $\frac{25}{216}$ | $\frac{5}{36}$ | $\frac{1}{6}$ |

**[A1 A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: The values −2, −1, 0, 1 and 3 only, in a table or listed.
> 
> **M1**: A probability found as `\left(\dfrac{5}{6}\right)^{r-1} \times \dfrac{1}{6}` (the lucky number first appearing on roll $r$) for at least two values of $W$.
> 
> **A1**: At least three probabilities correct.
> 
> **A1**: All five probabilities correct, including `\text{P}(W = -2) = \left(\dfrac{5}{6}\right)^{4}`. Equivalent fractions over 1296 and decimals correct to 3 significant figures are accepted.

parts.problemMd:
Find the probability that, in one game, Leofranc

(i) wins money,

(ii) loses money,

(iii) breaks even (neither wins nor loses money).
parts.solutionMd:
| $w$ | −2 | −1 | 0 | 1 | 3 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $\text{P} ( W = w )$ | $\frac{625}{1296}$ | $\frac{125}{1296}$ | $\frac{25}{216}$ | $\frac{5}{36}$ | $\frac{1}{6}$ |

(i)

Winning money means a positive profit, $W = 1$ or $W = 3$

$\text{P} ( W > 0 ) = \frac{5}{36} + \frac{1}{6} = \frac{5}{36} + \frac{6}{36}$

$\text{P} ( \text{wins money} ) = \frac{11}{36}$

**[B1]**

(ii)

Losing money means a negative profit, $W = - 1$ or $W = - 2$

$\text{P} ( W < 0 ) = \frac{625}{1296} + \frac{125}{1296} = \frac{750}{1296}$

$\text{P} ( \text{loses money} ) = \frac{125}{216}$

**[B1]**

(iii)

Breaking even means $W = 0$

$\text{P} ( \text{breaks even} ) = \frac{25}{216}$

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: $\frac{11}{36}$, or answers which round to 0.306.
> 
> **B1**: $\frac{125}{216}$, or equivalent such as $\frac{750}{1296}$, or answers which round to 0.579.
> 
> **B1**: $\frac{25}{216}$, or answers which round to 0.116.

parts.problemMd: Find Leofranc's expected profit from one game.
parts.solutionMd:
| $w$ | −2 | −1 | 0 | 1 | 3 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $\text{P} ( W = w )$ | $\frac{625}{1296}$ | $\frac{125}{1296}$ | $\frac{25}{216}$ | $\frac{5}{36}$ | $\frac{1}{6}$ |

Use $\text{E} ( W ) = \sum w p$, with every probability over 1296

$\text{E} ( W ) = - 2 \times \frac{625}{1296} - 1 \times \frac{125}{1296} + 0 \times \frac{150}{1296} + 1 \times \frac{180}{1296} + 3 \times \frac{216}{1296}$

**[M1]**

$\text{E} ( W ) = \frac{-1250-125+180+648}{1296} = - \frac{547}{1296} = - 0 . 42206 \dots$

**Final answer:** $\text{E} ( W ) = - 0 . 422$** dollars (3 s.f.), a loss of about 42 cents**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: $\sum w p$ with all five terms from the table. Accept unsimplified.
> 
> **A1**: $- \frac{547}{1296}$, or answers which round to $- 0 . 422$. A loss of 0.422 dollars (or 42 cents) is equivalent. Units are not required.

parts.problemMd:
The discrete random variable $X$ has the probability distribution shown in the following table.

| $x$ | −3 | −2 | −1 | 0 | 1 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $\text{P} ( X = x )$ | $p$ | $q$ | 0.1 | $q$ | $p$ |

Write down the value of $\text{E} ( X )$.
parts.solutionMd:
The values and their probabilities are symmetrical about $- 1$

$\text{E} ( X ) = - 1$

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: $\text{E} ( X ) = - 1$.

parts.problemMd:
It is given that $\text{E} ( X^{2} ) = 3 . 4$.

Find $\text{Var} ( X )$.
parts.solutionMd:
Use `\text{Var}(X) = \text{E}(X^{2}) - \left[\text{E}(X)\right]^{2}`

`\text{Var}(X) = 3.4 - \left(-1\right)^{2}`

$\text{Var} ( X ) = 2 . 4$

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: 2.4, using the value of $\text{E} ( X )$ from part (a) in `3.4 - \left[\text{E}(X)\right]^{2}`.

parts.problemMd: Find the value of $p$ and the value of $q$.
parts.solutionMd:
The probabilities sum to 1

$p + q + 0 . 1 + q + p = 1$

$p + q = 0 . 45$

**[B1]**

Use $\text{E} ( X^{2} ) = \sum x^{2} p$ and set it equal to 3.4

`\left(-3\right)^{2}p + \left(-2\right)^{2}q + \left(-1\right)^{2} \times 0.1 + 0^{2} \times q + 1^{2} \times p = 3.4`

$10 p + 4 q + 0 . 1 = 3 . 4$

$5 p + 2 q = 1 . 65$

**[B1]**

Multiply the first equation by 2

$2 p + 2 q = 0 . 9$

Subtract this from $5 p + 2 q = 1 . 65$ to eliminate $q$

$3 p = 0 . 75$

**[M1]**

$p = 0 . 25$

Substitute into $p + q = 0 . 45$

$p = 0 . 25 ,  q = 0 . 2$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: $p + q = 0 . 45$, or any equivalent, from the probabilities summing to 1 or from $\text{E} ( X ) = - 1$.
> 
> **B1**: A correct equation from $\text{E} ( X^{2} ) = 3 . 4$, with all five terms, simplified or unsimplified (e.g. $10 p + 4 q + 0 . 1 = 3 . 4$).
> 
> **M1**: Solving the two equations by substitution or elimination to find one of the unknowns.
> 
> **A1**: $p = 0 . 25$ and $q = 0 . 2$.

parts.problemMd:
A spinner has three sectors labelled 0, 1 and 2. The random variable $X$ denotes the number that the spinner lands on when it is spun. The probability distribution table for $X$ is shown below.

| $x$ | 0 | 1 | 2 |
|---|---|---|---|
| $\text{P} ( X = x )$ | $a$ | $b$ | $c$ |

It is given that $\text{E} ( X ) = 1 . 1$ and $\text{Var} ( X ) = 0 . 89$.

Find $\text{E} ( X^{2} )$.
parts.solutionMd:
Rearrange `\text{Var}(X) = \text{E}(X^{2}) - \left[\text{E}(X)\right]^{2}`

`\text{E}(X^{2}) = \text{Var}(X) + \left[\text{E}(X)\right]^{2} = 0.89 + 1.1^{2}`

$\text{E} ( X^{2} ) = 2 . 1$

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: $\text{E} ( X^{2} ) = 2 . 1$.

parts.problemMd: Find the values of $a$, $b$ and $c$.
parts.solutionMd:
Use $\text{E} ( X ) = \sum x p = 1 . 1$

$0 \times a + 1 \times b + 2 \times c = 1 . 1$

$b + 2 c = 1 . 1$

**[B1]**

Use $\text{E} ( X^{2} ) = \sum x^{2} p = 2 . 1$ from part (a)

$0^{2} \times a + 1^{2} \times b + 2^{2} \times c = 2 . 1$

$b + 4 c = 2 . 1$

**[B1]**

Subtract the first equation from the second

$2 c = 1$

**[M1]**

$c = 0 . 5$

$b = 1 . 1 - 2 \times 0 . 5 = 0 . 1$

The probabilities sum to 1

$a = 1 - 0 . 1 - 0 . 5 = 0 . 4$

$a = 0 . 4 ,  b = 0 . 1 ,  c = 0 . 5$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: $b + 2 c = 1 . 1$, or equivalent, from $\text{E} ( X ) = 1 . 1$.
> 
> **B1**: $b + 4 c = 2 . 1$, or equivalent, from the value of $\text{E} ( X^{2} )$ in part (a).
> 
> **M1**: Solving the two equations to find $b$ or $c$.
> 
> **A1**: $a = 0 . 4$, $b = 0 . 1$ and $c = 0 . 5$, with $a$ from the probabilities summing to 1.

parts.problemMd:
Susie spins the spinner twice and adds together the two numbers to calculate her score, $S$. Tommy spins the spinner once and doubles the number to calculate his score, $T$. Each spin of the spinner is independent of all other spins.

Draw up the probability distribution table for

(i) $S$,

(ii) $T$.
parts.solutionMd:
| $x$ | 0 | 1 | 2 |
|---|---|---|---|
| $\text{P} ( X = x )$ | 0.4 | 0.1 | 0.5 |

(i)

$S$ can be 0, 1, 2, 3 or 4. List the ordered pairs of spins for each total

**[B1 B1 B1]**

(ii)

$T$ is double one spin, so $T = 0 ,  2 \text{or} 4$ with the probabilities of $X = 0 ,  1 \text{or} 2$

| $t$ | **Final answer:** **0** | **Final answer:** **2** | **Final answer:** **4** |
|---|---|---|---|

parts.problemMd:
The random variable $X$ takes the values $p$, $2 p$, $3 p$, $4 p$ and $5 p$ only, where $p$ is a positive constant. It is given that $\text{P} ( X = x ) = \frac{x^{2}}{495}$.

Write each probability in terms of $p$ and set their sum equal to 1

$p = 3$

parts.problemMd:
Find

(i) the mean, $μ$,

(ii) the standard deviation, $σ$,

of $X$.
parts.solutionMd:
| $x$ | 3 | 6 | 9 | 12 | 15 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $\text{P} ( X = x )$ | $\frac{1}{55}$ | $\frac{4}{55}$ | $\frac{9}{55}$ | $\frac{16}{55}$ | $\frac{25}{55}$ |

(i)

Use $μ = \text{E} ( X ) = \sum x p$

$μ = \frac{3\times1+6\times4+9\times9+12\times16+15\times25}{55} = \frac{675}{55}$

**[M1]**

**Final answer:** $μ = \frac{135}{11} = 12 . 3$** (3 s.f.)**

**[A1]**

(ii)

Use $σ^{2} = \sum x^{2} p - μ^{2}$

`\sigma^{2} = \dfrac{3^{2} \times 1 + 6^{2} \times 4 + 9^{2} \times 9 + 12^{2} \times 16 + 15^{2} \times 25}{55} - \left(\dfrac{135}{11}\right)^{2}`

**[M1]**

`\sigma^{2} = \dfrac{8811}{55} - \left(\dfrac{135}{11}\right)^{2} = 160.2 - 150.6198\ldots = 9.58016\ldots`

$σ = \sqrt{9.58016\dots} = 3 . 09518 \dots$

**Final answer:** $σ = 3 . 10$** (3 s.f.)**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: $\sum x p$ with all five terms from the table. Accept unsimplified.
> 
> **A1**: $μ = \frac{135}{11}$, or answers which round to 12.3.
> 
> **M1**: $\sum x^{2} p$ minus the square of the mean. Accept unsimplified.
> 
> **A1**: Standard deviation which rounds to 3.10.

parts.solutionMd:

The only values of $X$ between 9.18 and 15.37 are 12 and 15

(iv) On the first spin, it is a 'win' if the spinner lands on an even number. On subsequent spins it is a 'win' if the spinner lands *either* on the same number as the previous spin *or* on a factor of the number from the previous spin. parts.solutionMd:

**Final answer:** **Binomial: **`Y \sim \text{B}\left(12, \; \dfrac{1}{2}\right)`

**[B1]**

**[B1]**

> 
> **B1**: $W$ not binomial, with a reason (not a fixed number of trials).
> 
> **B1**: $Y$ binomial, with a reason (12 independent spins, constant probability of a prime). Accept B(12, 0.5) as the reason.

> **B1**: $L$ not binomial, with a reason (the probability of a win depends on the previous spin; not constant; not independent).

parts.problemMd:
It is known that 40% of the seeds of a certain variety germinate. A random sample of 500 of these seeds is sown.

Use an approximation to find the probability that the number of these seeds that germinate is between 189 and 211 inclusive.
parts.solutionMd:
The 500 seeds germinate independently, each with probability 0.4, so $W$, the number that germinate, follows a binomial distribution

`W \sim \text{B}(500, \; 0.4)`

For the normal approximation, the mean is $n p$ and the variance is $n p ( 1 - p )$

$μ = 500 \times 0 . 4 = 200$

$σ^{2} = 500 \times 0 . 4 \times 0 . 6 = 120$

**[B1]**

Let $Y$ be the approximating normal variable

`Y \sim \text{N}(200, \; 120)`

"Between 189 and 211 inclusive" means the number that germinate can be any whole number from 189 to 211; on the continuous scale, $Y$ can take any value from 188.5 to 211.5 (continuity correction)

$\text{P} ( 189 \leq W \leq 211 ) \approx \text{P} ( 188 . 5 < Y < 211 . 5 )$

![Normal curve with the mean 200 marked by a dashed line and the area between 188.5 and 211.5 shaded](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-probability-and-statistics-1/statistical-distributions/working-with-distributions/assets/022-normal-curve-with-the-mean-200-marked-by-a-dashe.png)

Standardise using the formula

$Z = \frac{X-μ}{σ}$

Substitute $μ = 200$ and $σ = \sqrt{120}$

`\text{P}\left(\dfrac{188.5 - 200}{\sqrt{120}} < Z < \dfrac{211.5 - 200}{\sqrt{120}}\right) = \text{P}(-1.050 < Z < 1.050)`

**[M1 M1]**

The area between the two $z$-values is the area to the left of 1.050 minus the area to the left of −1.050

$\text{P} ( - 1 . 050 < Z < 1 . 050 ) = Φ ( 1 . 050 ) - Φ ( - 1 . 050 )$

The table only gives positive values of $z$. By symmetry, the area to the left of −1.050 equals the area to the right of 1.050

$Φ ( - 1 . 050 ) = 1 - Φ ( 1 . 050 )$

Substitute this into the first line

`\text{P}(-1.050 < Z < 1.050) = \mathrm{\Phi}(1.050) - \left(1 - \mathrm{\Phi}(1.050)\right)`

$\text{P} ( - 1 . 050 < Z < 1 . 050 ) = 2 Φ ( 1 . 050 ) - 1$

**[M1]**

In the table of the normal distribution function in the formula booklet, the 1.0 row and the 5 column give 0.8531

$2 \times 0 . 8531 - 1 = 0 . 7062$

**Final answer:** $\text{P} ( 189 \leq W \leq 211 ) = 0 . 706$** (3 s.f.)**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: Mean 200 and variance 120 seen, allow unsimplified. σ = 10.95 implies the variance. Giving 120 as the standard deviation does not score.
> 
> **M1**: Substituting their mean and their standard deviation into the standardisation formula (any boundary value), not σ² and not √σ.

> **M1**: A continuity correction: 188.5 or 189.5, and 210.5 or 211.5, in their standardisation.

parts.problemMd:
In a computer game, the probability that a player wins any round is $\frac{9}{19}$, independently of all other rounds.

For a random sample of 30 rounds, find the probability that the player wins exactly 14 rounds.
parts.solutionMd:
The 30 rounds are independent, each won with probability $\frac{9}{19}$, so $X$, the number of rounds won, follows a binomial distribution

`X \sim \text{B}\left(30, \; \dfrac{9}{19}\right)`

Use the binomial probability formula

`\text{P}(X = r) = {}^{n}C_{r} p^{r} (1 - p)^{n - r}`

`\text{P}(X = 14) = {}^{30}C_{14}\left(\dfrac{9}{19}\right)^{14}\left(\dfrac{10}{19}\right)^{16}`

**[M1]**

$\text{P} ( X = 14 ) = 0 . 144350 \dots$

**Final answer:** $\text{P} ( X = 14 ) = 0 . 144$** (3 s.f.)**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: A term of the form `{}^{30}C_{14}\,p^{14}(1 - p)^{16}`, 0 < p < 1.
> 
> **A1**: 0.144, or answers which round to 0.144.
> 
> If 0.144 is given with no working, for example straight from a calculator, award 1 mark only.

Standardise using the formula

**[M1 M1]**

The required area is to the right of 1.635

**[M1]**

In the table of the normal distribution function in the formula booklet, the 1.6 row and the 3 column give 0.9484, and ADD 5 in the 1.6 row is 5

$Φ ( 1 . 635 ) = 0 . 9484 + 0 . 0005 = 0 . 9489$

$1 - 0 . 9489 = 0 . 0511$

**Final answer:** $\text{P} ( Y \geq 500 ) = 0 . 0511$** (3 s.f.)**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: Mean 473.7 and variance 249.3 seen, allow unsimplified (such as $1000 \times \frac{9}{19}$). σ = 15.79 implies the variance. Giving 249.3 as the standard deviation does not score.

> 
> **M1**: A continuity correction of 499.5 or 500.5 in their standardisation.

> **M1**: The appropriate area, 1 − Φ(1.635), which must be a probability less than 0.5.

parts.problemMd:

parts.problemMd:
The weights, in grams, of the chocolate bars produced by a certain manufacturer are normally distributed with mean 200 and standard deviation 17.5.

Find the probability that a randomly chosen chocolate bar weighs less than 195 grams.
parts.solutionMd:

$Z = \frac{X-μ}{σ}$

Substitute $X = 195$, $μ = 200$ and $σ = 17 . 5$

`\text{P}(W < 195) = \text{P}\left(Z < \dfrac{195 - 200}{17.5}\right) = \text{P}(Z < -0.286)`

**[M1]**

The $z$-value is negative, so use symmetry

$\text{P} ( Z < - 0 . 286 ) = 1 - Φ ( 0 . 286 )$

**[M1]**

In the table of the normal distribution function in the formula booklet, the 0.2 row and the 8 column give 0.6103, and ADD 6 in the 0.2 row is 23

$Φ ( 0 . 286 ) = 0 . 6103 + 0 . 0023 = 0 . 6126$

$1 - 0 . 6126 = 0 . 3874$

**Final answer:** $\text{P} ( W < 195 ) = 0 . 387$** (3 s.f.)**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Standardising with 195, 200 and 17.5. Using 17.5² or √17.5, or a continuity correction, does not score.
> 
> **M1**: The appropriate area, 1 − Φ(0.286) or Φ(−0.286), leading to a probability less than 0.5.

parts.problemMd:

parts.problemMd:
A machine produces plastic counters. Each counter is red with probability $\frac{6}{13}$, black with probability $\frac{6}{13}$, and otherwise green, independently of all other counters.

A random sample of 50 counters is chosen. Find the probability that exactly 45 of these counters are either red or black.
parts.solutionMd:
A counter is red or black with probability

$\frac{6}{13} + \frac{6}{13} = \frac{12}{13}$

The 50 counters are independent, so $X$, the number that are red or black, follows a binomial distribution

`X \sim \text{B}\left(50, \; \dfrac{12}{13}\right)`

Use the binomial probability formula

`\text{P}(X = r) = {}^{n}C_{r} p^{r} (1 - p)^{n - r}`

`\text{P}(X = 45) = {}^{50}C_{45}\left(\dfrac{12}{13}\right)^{45}\left(\dfrac{1}{13}\right)^{5}`

**[M1]**

$\text{P} ( X = 45 ) = 0 . 155621 \dots$

**Final answer:** $\text{P} ( X = 45 ) = 0 . 156$** (3 s.f.)**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: A term of the form `{}^{50}C_{45}\,p^{45}(1 - p)^{5}`, 0 < p < 1.
> 
> **A1**: 0.156, or answers which round to 0.156.
> 
> If 0.156 is given with no working, for example straight from a calculator, award 1 mark only.

parts.problemMd:
In a separate experiment, a random sample of 1000 counters is chosen.

Use a suitable approximation to find the probability that at least 75 but fewer than 80 of these counters are green.
parts.solutionMd:
A counter is green with probability $1 - \frac{12}{13} = \frac{1}{13}$, so $Y$, the number of green counters, follows `\text{B}\left(1000, \; \dfrac{1}{13}\right)`; for the normal approximation, the mean is $n p$ and the variance is $n p ( 1 - p )$

$μ = 1000 \times \frac{1}{13} = 76 . 923 \dots$

$σ^{2} = 1000 \times \frac{1}{13} \times \frac{12}{13} = 71 . 005 \dots$

**[B1]**

"At least 75 but fewer than 80" means the number of green counters can be any whole number from 75 to 79; on the continuous scale, with `V \sim \text{N}(76.923\ldots, \; 71.005\ldots)`, $V$ can take any value from 74.5 to 79.5 (continuity correction)

$\text{P} ( 75 \leq Y < 80 ) \approx \text{P} ( 74 . 5 < V < 79 . 5 )$

![Normal curve with the mean 76.9 marked by a dashed line and the area between 74.5 and 79.5 shaded](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-probability-and-statistics-1/statistical-distributions/working-with-distributions/assets/014-normal-curve-with-the-mean-76-9-marked-by-a-dash.png)

Standardise each boundary using the formula

$Z = \frac{X-μ}{σ}$

Substitute $σ = \sqrt{71.005\dots} = 8 . 4265 \dots$

`\text{P}\left(\dfrac{74.5 - 76.923\ldots}{8.4265\ldots} < Z < \dfrac{79.5 - 76.923\ldots}{8.4265\ldots}\right) = \text{P}(-0.288 < Z < 0.306)`

**[M1 M1]**

The area is the area to the left of 0.306 minus the area to the left of −0.288, using symmetry for the negative value

`\text{P}(-0.288 < Z < 0.306) = \mathrm{\Phi}(0.306) - \left(1 - \mathrm{\Phi}(0.288)\right)`

**[M1]**

In the table of the normal distribution function in the formula booklet, the 0.3 row and the 0 column give 0.6179, and ADD 6 in the 0.3 row is 22

$Φ ( 0 . 306 ) = 0 . 6179 + 0 . 0022 = 0 . 6201$

The 0.2 row and the 8 column give 0.6103, and ADD 8 in the 0.2 row is 31

$Φ ( 0 . 288 ) = 0 . 6103 + 0 . 0031 = 0 . 6134$

$0 . 6201 - ( 1 - 0 . 6134 ) = 0 . 2335$

**Final answer:** $\text{P} ( 75 \leq Y < 80 ) = 0 . 234$** (3 s.f.)**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: Mean 76.92 and variance 71.01 seen, allow unsimplified. σ = 8.427 implies the variance. Giving 71.01 as the standard deviation does not score.
> 
> **M1**: Substituting their mean and their standard deviation into the standardisation formula (any boundary value), not σ² and not √σ.
> 
> **M1**: Continuity corrections: 74.5 or 75.5, and 78.5 or 79.5, in their standardisation.
> 
> **M1**: The appropriate area from their z-values, such as Φ(0.306) − (1 − Φ(0.288)), which must be a probability.
> 
> **A1**: 0.233 or 0.234 (table or calculator values of Φ), accepting any value from 0.233 to 0.2335.
>

parts.problemMd:
At a large supermarket, 60% of customers pay by card. A random sample of 1200 customers is chosen.

Use a suitable approximation to find the probability that the number of these customers who pay by card is more than 700 and at most 730.
parts.solutionMd:
The 1200 customers are chosen at random, so they are independent, each paying by card with probability 0.6; so $W$, the number who pay by card, follows a binomial distribution, `W \sim \text{B}(1200, \; 0.6)`; for the normal approximation, the mean is $n p$ and the variance is $n p ( 1 - p )$

$μ = 1200 \times 0 . 6 = 720$

$σ^{2} = 1200 \times 0 . 6 \times 0 . 4 = 288$

**[B1]**

"More than 700 and at most 730" means the number who pay by card can be any whole number from 701 to 730; on the continuous scale, with `V \sim \text{N}(720, \; 288)`, $V$ can take any value from 700.5 to 730.5 (continuity correction)

$\text{P} ( 700 < W \leq 730 ) \approx \text{P} ( 700 . 5 < V < 730 . 5 )$

![Normal curve with the mean 720 marked by a dashed line and the area between 700.5 and 730.5 shaded](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-probability-and-statistics-1/statistical-distributions/working-with-distributions/assets/016-normal-curve-with-the-mean-720-marked-by-a-dashe.png)

Standardise each boundary using the formula

$Z = \frac{X-μ}{σ}$

Substitute $σ = \sqrt{288} = 16 . 970 \dots$

`\text{P}\left(\dfrac{700.5 - 720}{\sqrt{288}} < Z < \dfrac{730.5 - 720}{\sqrt{288}}\right) = \text{P}(-1.149 < Z < 0.619)`

**[M1 M1]**

The area is the area to the left of 0.619 minus the area to the left of −1.149, using symmetry for the negative value

`\text{P}(-1.149 < Z < 0.619) = \mathrm{\Phi}(0.619) - \left(1 - \mathrm{\Phi}(1.149)\right)`

**[M1]**

In the table of the normal distribution function in the formula booklet, the 0.6 row and the 1 column give 0.7291, and ADD 9 in the 0.6 row is 29

$Φ ( 0 . 619 ) = 0 . 7291 + 0 . 0029 = 0 . 7320$

The 1.1 row and the 4 column give 0.8729, and ADD 9 in the 1.1 row is 18

$Φ ( 1 . 149 ) = 0 . 8729 + 0 . 0018 = 0 . 8747$

$0 . 7320 - ( 1 - 0 . 8747 ) = 0 . 6067$

**Final answer:** $\text{P} ( 700 < W \leq 730 ) = 0 . 607$** (3 s.f.)**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: Mean 720 and variance 288 seen, allow unsimplified. σ = 16.97 implies the variance. Giving 288 as the standard deviation does not score.
> 
> **M1**: Substituting their mean and their standard deviation into the standardisation formula (any boundary value), not σ² and not √σ.
> 
> **M1**: Continuity corrections: 700.5 or 701.5, and 729.5 or 730.5, in their standardisation.
> 
> **M1**: The appropriate area from their z-values, such as Φ(0.619) − (1 − Φ(1.149)), which must be a probability.
> 
> **A1**: 0.607, accepting any value from 0.6065 to 0.607.
> 
> If the answer is given with no working, for example straight from a calculator, award 1 mark only.

parts.problemMd: Use your approximation to find the probability that at least 719 of these customers pay by card.
parts.solutionMd:
"At least 719" means the number can be any whole number from 719 upwards; on the continuous scale, $V$ can take any value above 718.5

$\text{P} ( W \geq 719 ) \approx \text{P} ( V > 718 . 5 )$

![Normal curve with the mean 720 marked by a dashed line and the area to the right of 718.5 shaded](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-probability-and-statistics-1/statistical-distributions/working-with-distributions/assets/017-normal-curve-with-the-mean-720-marked-by-a-dashe.png)

Standardise using the formula

$Z = \frac{X-μ}{σ}$

Substitute $μ = 720$ and $σ = \sqrt{288}$

`\text{P}\left(Z > \dfrac{718.5 - 720}{\sqrt{288}}\right) = \text{P}(Z > -0.088)`

**[M1]**

By symmetry, the area to the right of −0.088 equals the area to the left of 0.088

$\text{P} ( Z > - 0 . 088 ) = Φ ( 0 . 088 )$

**[M1]**

In the table of the normal distribution function in the formula booklet, the 0.0 row and the 8 column give 0.5319, and ADD 8 in the 0.0 row is 32

$Φ ( 0 . 088 ) = 0 . 5319 + 0 . 0032 = 0 . 5351$

**Final answer:** $\text{P} ( W \geq 719 ) = 0 . 535$** (3 s.f.)**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Standardising with their mean and standard deviation and a continuity correction of 718.5 or 719.5.
> 
> **M1**: The appropriate area, Φ(0.088), leading to a probability greater than 0.5.
> 
> **A1**: 0.535, accepting any value from 0.535 to 0.5355.
> 
> If the answer is given with no working, for example straight from a calculator, award 1 mark only.

parts.solutionMd:
A normal approximation to $\text{B} ( n ,  p )$ is valid when $n p > 5$ and $n ( 1 - p ) > 5$

parts.problemMd: Using your approximation, find the greatest integer value of $k$ such that the probability that the number of these customers who pay by card differs from 720 by less than $k$ is less than 0.5.
parts.solutionMd:
The number differs from 720 by less than $k$ when it is any whole number from $721 - k$ to $719 + k$; on the continuous scale, $V$ can take any value from $720 . 5 - k$ to $719 . 5 + k$, which is $k - 0 . 5$ either side of the mean

$\text{P} ( 720 . 5 - k < V < 719 . 5 + k ) < 0 . 5$

![Normal curve with the mean 720 marked by a dashed line and a symmetrical area of 0.5 shaded between 720.5 − k and 719.5 + k](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-probability-and-statistics-1/statistical-distributions/working-with-distributions/assets/018-normal-curve-with-the-mean-720-marked-by-a-dashe.png)

Standardise using the formula

$Z = \frac{X-μ}{σ}$

Let $c = \frac{k-0.5}{\sqrt{288}}$; the interval standardises to $- c < Z < c$, and its area is the area to the left of $c$ minus the area to the left of $- c$

$\text{P} ( - c < Z < c ) = Φ ( c ) - Φ ( - c )$

By symmetry, the area to the left of $- c$ equals the area to the right of $c$

$Φ ( - c ) = 1 - Φ ( c )$

`\text{P}(-c < Z < c) = \mathrm{\Phi}(c) - \left(1 - \mathrm{\Phi}(c)\right) = 2\mathrm{\Phi}(c) - 1`

**[M1]**

Set this less than 0.5

$2 Φ ( c ) - 1 < 0 . 5$

$Φ ( c ) < 0 . 75$

0.75 is in the table of critical values in the formula booklet

$z = 0 . 674$

**[B1]**

$\frac{k-0.5}{\sqrt{288}} < 0 . 674$

**[M1]**

$k < 0 . 5 + 0 . 674 \sqrt{288} = 11 . 938 \dots$

$k$ is an integer

$k = 11$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: The symmetrical area written as 2Φ(z) − 1 (or equivalent) for an interval centred on 720.
> 
> **B1**: z = 0.674, the critical value for 0.75.
> 
> **M1**: (k − 0.5)/√288 (or k/√288 with no continuity correction, or k + 0.5) compared with or equated to their z-value. Using 0.75 or 0.25 as z does not score.
> 
> **A1**: k = 11 only.

parts.problemMd:
The probability that a seed of a certain type produces a red flower is $\frac{18}{37}$.

A random sample of 36 seeds of this type is chosen. Find the probability that exactly 18 of these seeds produce red flowers.
parts.solutionMd:
The 36 seeds are chosen at random, so they are independent, each producing a red flower with probability $\frac{18}{37}$; so $X$, the number of seeds producing red flowers, follows a binomial distribution

`X \sim \text{B}\left(36, \; \dfrac{18}{37}\right)`

Use the binomial probability formula

`\text{P}(X = r) = {}^{n}C_{r} p^{r} (1 - p)^{n - r}`

`\text{P}(X = 18) = {}^{36}C_{18}\left(\dfrac{18}{37}\right)^{18}\left(\dfrac{19}{37}\right)^{18}`

**[M1]**

$\text{P} ( X = 18 ) = 0 . 130334 \dots$

**Final answer:** $\text{P} ( X = 18 ) = 0 . 130$** (3 s.f.)**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: A term of the form `{}^{36}C_{18}\,p^{18}(1 - p)^{18}`, 0 < p < 1.
> 
> **A1**: 0.130, or answers which round to 0.130.
>

parts.problemMd:
In a separate experiment, a random sample of 1000 seeds of this type is chosen.

Use a suitable approximation to find the probability that fewer than 482 or more than 491 of these seeds produce red flowers.
parts.solutionMd:
Let $Y$ be the number of these seeds producing red flowers, so `Y \sim \text{B}\left(1000, \; \dfrac{18}{37}\right)`; for the normal approximation, the mean is $n p$ and the variance is $n p ( 1 - p )$

$μ = 1000 \times \frac{18}{37} = 486 . 486 \dots$

$σ^{2} = 1000 \times \frac{18}{37} \times \frac{19}{37} = 249 . 817 \dots$

**[B1]**

"Fewer than 482" means the number can be any whole number up to 481, and "more than 491" means any whole number from 492 upwards; on the continuous scale, with `V \sim \text{N}(486.486\ldots, \; 249.817\ldots)`, $V$ can take any value below 481.5 or above 491.5 (continuity correction)

$\text{P} ( Y < 482 \text{or} Y > 491 ) \approx \text{P} ( V < 481 . 5 ) + \text{P} ( V > 491 . 5 )$

![Normal curve with the mean 486.5 marked by a dashed line and both tails shaded: to the left of 481.5 and to the right of 491.5](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-probability-and-statistics-1/statistical-distributions/working-with-distributions/assets/015-normal-curve-with-the-mean-486-5-marked-by-a-das.png)

Standardise each boundary using the formula

$Z = \frac{X-μ}{σ}$

Substitute $σ = \sqrt{249.817\dots} = 15 . 806 \dots$

`\text{P}(V < 481.5) = \text{P}\left(Z < \dfrac{481.5 - 486.486\ldots}{15.806\ldots}\right) = \text{P}(Z < -0.315)`

`\text{P}(V > 491.5) = \text{P}\left(Z > \dfrac{491.5 - 486.486\ldots}{15.806\ldots}\right) = \text{P}(Z > 0.317)`

**[M1 M1]**

Each tail is 1 minus a value from the table (using symmetry for the left tail)

`\text{P}(Z < -0.315) + \text{P}(Z > 0.317) = \left(1 - \mathrm{\Phi}(0.315)\right) + \left(1 - \mathrm{\Phi}(0.317)\right)`

**[M1]**

In the table of the normal distribution function in the formula booklet, the 0.3 row and the 1 column give 0.6217; ADD 5 in that row is 19 and ADD 7 is 26

$Φ ( 0 . 315 ) = 0 . 6217 + 0 . 0019 = 0 . 6236$

$Φ ( 0 . 317 ) = 0 . 6217 + 0 . 0026 = 0 . 6243$

$( 1 - 0 . 6236 ) + ( 1 - 0 . 6243 ) = 0 . 3764 + 0 . 3757 = 0 . 7521$

**Final answer:** $\text{P} ( Y < 482 \text{or} Y > 491 ) = 0 . 752$** (3 s.f.)**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: Mean 486.5 and variance 249.8 seen, allow unsimplified. σ = 15.81 implies the variance. Giving 249.8 as the standard deviation does not score.
> 
> **M1**: Substituting their mean and their standard deviation into at least one standardisation (any boundary value), not σ² and not √σ.
> 
> **M1**: Continuity corrections: 481.5 or 482.5, and 490.5 or 491.5, in their two standardisations.
> 
> **M1**: The appropriate area for both tails, such as (1 − Φ(0.315)) + (1 − Φ(0.317)) or 1 − (Φ(0.317) − Φ(−0.315)), which must be a probability.
> 
> **A1**: 0.752, accepting any value from 0.7515 to 0.7525.
> 
> If the answer is given with no working, for example straight from a calculator, award 1 mark only.

parts.problemMd:
The weights of the feed in sacks of partridge feed produced by a certain manufacturer are normally distributed with mean 20 kg and standard deviation 0.1 kg.

Find the probability that a randomly chosen sack contains less than 19.75 kg of feed.
parts.solutionMd:

Standardise using the formula

$Z = \frac{X-μ}{σ}$

Substitute $X = 19 . 75$, $μ = 20$ and $σ = 0 . 1$

`\text{P}(W < 19.75) = \text{P}\left(Z < \dfrac{19.75 - 20}{0.1}\right) = \text{P}(Z < -2.5)`

**[M1]**

The $z$-value is negative, so use symmetry

$\text{P} ( Z < - 2 . 5 ) = 1 - Φ ( 2 . 5 )$

**[M1]**

In the table of the normal distribution function in the formula booklet, the 2.5 row and the 0 column give 0.9938

$1 - 0 . 9938 = 0 . 0062$

$\text{P} ( W < 19 . 75 ) = 0 . 0062$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Standardising with 19.75, 20 and 0.1. Using 0.01 (the variance) or √0.1 does not score.
> 
> **M1**: The appropriate area, 1 − Φ(2.5), leading to a probability less than 0.5.

parts.problemMd:

parts.solutionMd:
A weight differs from 20 kg by less than 0.25 kg when it is between 19.75 kg and 20.25 kg; the normal curve is symmetrical about 20, so the area above 20.25 equals the area below 19.75 found in part (a)

![Normal curve with the mean 20 marked by a dashed line, the area between 19.75 and 20.25 shaded, and the two equal tails each labelled 0.0062](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-probability-and-statistics-1/statistical-distributions/working-with-distributions/assets/020-normal-curve-with-the-mean-20-marked-by-a-dashed.png)

$\text{P} ( 19 . 75 < W < 20 . 25 ) = 1 - 2 \times \text{P} ( W < 19 . 75 )$

**[M1]**

$1 - 2 \times 0 . 0062 = 0 . 9876$

**[A1]**

The 10 sacks are chosen at random, so they are independent, and each must be within 0.25 kg of the mean

$0 . 9876^{10} = 0 . 88269 \dots$

**Final answer:** $0 . 883$** (3 s.f.)**

> 
> **A1**: 0.9876, or answers which round to 0.988, kept to at least 4 s.f. for the next step.
